`chains.js` derives production dependencies and compatible destinations from the economy catalogs. `chains-view.js` and `chains.css` present the current environment's complete graph, an output's recursive ingredient chain, and every world instance of a selected industry type. Locating an instance centers the map and opens its inspector. The inspector shows downstream cargo consumers and up to five closest matching industry or town destinations. Distances describe direct map distance, not a verified road, rail or water connection.

`route-planner.js` provides the DOM-free route filtering and connection validation used by the Routes panel. The panel keeps its text search and mode/status/cargo filters separate from the route draft. Native station selectors remain available alongside map picking. Selecting a departure on the map advances to arrival selection; only stations matching the route's transport mode are accepted. Cancel, Escape and changing away from Routes end the picker. On mobile, choosing the final stop reopens the management panel.

The route planner verifies the actual network and station cargo coverage before launch. Its cached path result is invalidated by selected stops, transport mode or `networkRevision`; changes to available funds and cargo eligibility also update launch availability. The simulation's `addRoute` still performs authoritative validation when the form is submitted.

`compact-hud.css` fits navigation, finances, date and speed into one header row. Company delivery and connection totals are exposed through the finances button's hover/focus/click tooltip. `industry-targets.css` keeps the expanded industry inspector scrollable within the map on desktop and mobile.

## Local save slots

The automatic checkpoint keeps the existing `transport-save-v1` key and compact tile format. Named snapshots use one independent `transport-slot-v1:<id>` localStorage entry per slot; listing enumerates this prefix without a separate index. Each versioned envelope includes its id, name, biome, game day, balance, save timestamp, dimensions, route count, payload encoding, checksum and complete compact game payload. Native gzip compresses a `tile-binary-v1` frame with raw packed tile bytes before base64 encoding for original sizes or dense 15-bit UTF16 packing for Vast; JSON remains the fallback when compression is unavailable. The payload checksum lets listing flag accidental edits and truncation without expanding each world.

`save-slots.js` provides `listSaveSlots()`, asynchronous `writeSaveSlot(game, {id?, name})` and `readSaveSlot(id)`, plus `renameSaveSlot(id, name)` and `deleteSaveSlot(id)`. List metadata distinguishes ready, corrupt and unavailable entries. The autosave has id `autosave` and is read-only through this API. Writes validate and serialize before a single `setItem`, preserving the previous record when storage rejects a write. Renaming changes metadata without re-encoding its payload. Reading validates and hydrates the complete world but does not activate it or change storage.

`saves-view.js` and `saves.css` mount the Load / save dialog with named slots, an independent autosave checkpoint, asynchronous progress/errors, and inline confirmations for replacing the world, overwriting a slot or deleting one. Disposal prevents an outstanding read from activating a company after the dialog has closed. The dialog retains an accessible close control while operations run and while its list scrolls.

`app.js` activates a loaded or generated world only after writing its new autosave successfully. New-world generation paints a progress state before synchronous generation and disables duplicate submission. Atlas/minimap geometry follows the current world aspect ratio. Activation refreshes the renderer, minimap, camera, tool, route draft and filters, inspector and chain selection. Failed activation leaves the current company and prior autosave intact. The dialog pauses the simulation and periodic autosaving; the previous simulation speed resumes on closing. Named saves are independent snapshots and are not updated by periodic autosave or new-world generation.

## Map visibility

`visibility.js` defines thirteen independent display preferences: `trees`, `buildings`, `roads`, `rails`, `stations`, `names`, `industryIcons`, `vehicles`, `vehicleLoads`, `routes`, `zones`, `lighting` and `grid`. Defaults enable every layer, including the gentle grid. `layerPreset('all')` enables all thirteen, while `layerPreset('terrain')` disables all thirteen. Normalization accepts only known boolean fields. Browser persistence uses `transport-visibility-v1`, independently of both the active autosave and named game slots; read/write failures leave the current interface usable.

`visibility-view.js` and `visibility.css` present a nonmodal popover with native labeled checkbox switches, presets, keyboard support and outside/Escape dismissal. It reads current flags through callbacks and delegates changes to `app.js`, without touching simulation state. Opening this panel does not pause the game. Loading or generating a company retains the existing display preferences.

`renderer.js` applies scenery/network flags to cached terrain composition. Changing trees, buildings, roads, railways, stations or zones invalidates baked chunks across zoom levels. Names, industry icons, vehicles, load indicators, routes and the grid are live overlays. Vegetation includes forest sprites and plant details; sparse rocks remain scenery, while mountains use the ground geometry. Buildings includes houses, civic structures and industry art. Roads, rails and stops remain independently controllable. Hidden vehicles never draw load indicators, while hiding only their loads retains the vehicles.

`getStats().layers` exposes a copy of renderer preferences alongside cache and vehicle-indicator statistics. Legacy `render(now, {showGrid, showRoutes})` arguments remain optional per-render overrides and do not rewrite stored preferences. The minimap and atlas reflect applicable scenery/network flags. Hidden industry icons no longer contribute extended inspection hitboxes; hidden stop badges likewise lose their extended map-picker hitboxes. Their actual tiles remain inspectable and all gameplay occupancy/network rules remain intact. Selection, coverage and construction previews are contextual interaction overlays rather than persistent layers.

## Rivers and shipping

World generation carves connected water channels with `detail: 'river'`, joins tributaries to the trunk rivers and connects river mouths to sea. A navigable river runs beside both starter towns, with shoreline berths within the existing five-tile catchment. Generated streets preserve water and mark crossings as bridges; building placement skips water. River detail uses the existing lossless detail palette without a save format change. Existing saved terrain is not regenerated.

`build(game, 'port', x, y)` creates a water-mode station on unoccupied water cardinally adjacent to land. Ports cannot overlap bridges or other structures. `findPath(..., 'water')` follows cardinally connected water, including bridge tiles, and requires no network flags. Ports share `stationCoverage`, freight recipes, passenger eligibility, route validation, load/unload and saved state with land transport. A ship costs $64,000 and carries 140 units; a port costs $18,000. Water travel uses a slower base speed with seeded weather, shoreline, bridge-approach and port-traffic effects; port loading pauses and upkeep use the same deterministic simulation clocks.

The route planner, filters, map picking, port inspector and save validation accept the water mode. Ship and ferry rendering respects the Vehicles and Cargo loads switches; ports follow Stops. Ships pass under the visible bridge deck, while road and rail vehicles render above it. Port badges retain the existing 14-pixel station hitbox, using an anchor rather than the bus/train letter.

## Annual economy and vehicle generations

`economy-pricing.js` derives Gregorian years from the same January 1950 epoch as the HUD. `inflationInfo(game)` returns calendar year, year index, the seeded annual rate and the compound price index. `priceFor(game, basePrice)` rounds the current price. Rates and unlocked vehicle levels derive from seed and simulation day, requiring no new persisted schedule. A bounded cached calculation handles far-future saves. Monthly financial reports use Gregorian month boundaries from the same epoch. Construction, clearing surcharges, purchases, upgrades, upkeep and delivery revenue share this pricing layer; arrival revenue uses the actual arrival day.

`getVehiclePurchase` quotes the latest generation. Each calendar year unlocks one level, increasing base capacity by 20% and base speed by 10% per level. `getVehicleUpgrade` and `getFleetUpgrade` provide read-only quotes; `upgradeRouteVehicle` and `upgradeFleet` perform authoritative affordability checks and mutate the eligible fleet atomically. Vehicles store `level` and `paidPrice`, and retain load, position, progress and dwell time when upgraded. Legacy vehicles default to level zero and their original base purchase price. Retirement returns 45% of paid price, including upgrades. The UI refreshes quotes with calendar and funds changes.

## Biome scenery and lighting

`BIOME_NATURE` in `terrain-sprites.js` shares tree, mountain and plant catalogs between seeded world generation and local ecology. Expanded detail strings preserve the seven gameplay terrain classes and use the existing tile codec. Habitat patches choose related species; new woodland often inherits nearby species. `isPlantDetail` identifies decorative vegetation for rendering and environmental calculations. Hiding trees removes foothill vegetation while retaining the mountain itself.

`tree-sprites.js` generates 64 deterministic woodland compositions per biome/detail, containing one to five trees with per-tree species, leaf coverage, height, placement and branch/crown seeds. Composition is independent of zoom; each profile only adjusts fine marks. The renderer hashes tile coordinates, world seed and the saved variant into the artwork seed, so legacy 16-variant maps gain the new art without changing save state. Forest canvases are 48×48 logical pixels (x −8…40, y −16…32); their crowns can overlap neighboring cells. Other sprites keep the 32×40 envelope. Chunk padding covers these overhangs.

`relief-sprites.js` draws irregular mountain crests, layered desert formations and fractured boulders. `terrain-sprites.js` separates geometry and texture streams for stable vegetation between zooms. Nature uses 64 cached variants, other art retains 12; the sprite factory has a 16 MiB LRU limit in addition to the chunk budget.

`lighting.js` derives a 60-second cycle at 1× from saved simulation day, beginning at noon. A smooth ambient tint and cached glow sprites render after terrain and before screen-space labels. Windows, lamps, port reflections, headlights and navigation lights obey the matching visibility flags; the Lighting preference disables the pass for constant daytime. Lighting never advances the economy or invalidates baked terrain chunks. `hasClearableDecoration` keeps Bulldozer placement previews and authoritative cleanup consistent.

## Simple construction and map controls

`construction-plan.js` adapts the five-tool interface to existing model operations. `resolveBuildTool` chooses bridges/tunnels for Road/Rail and a station mode for Stop; explicit legacy tools still pass through. `quoteBuildPlan` deduplicates tiles and calls the authoritative construction quote. `buildPlan` delegates every placement to `model.build`, preserving single-placement metadata and the existing partial-success path policy. Renderer highlights resolve through the same adapter. The active tool never changes save structure or simulation rules.

`app.js` owns compact zoom/options popovers and the active-tool Done control. Every tool/view/dialog change cancels captured gestures. The gesture stores the original tool; releases cannot apply a subsequently chosen tool. Single-object dragging pans, while line tools build on release. A second touch cancels construction, pans with the midpoint and advances at most one of the three zooms per pinch gesture; releases remain inert until all touches lift. Space retains native button behavior, and a pan cannot also toggle pause. `controls.css` keeps map targets at least 44px and moves secondary options behind menus.

## Playability and accounting

`gameplay-insights.js` derives optional next projects, truthful town service, industry input/storage states and actionable route health. It uses the simulation’s five-tile station catchment and capacity-dependent900-unit storage. The interface keeps search/filter inputs mounted during periodic entity refresh, returns explicit view changes to the top, and exposes building benefits in the catalog and inspector.

Passenger loading and delivery share `passengerEndpoints`, selecting a distinct pair of covered towns by nearest combined walking distance. Homes record `populationCityId` to retain population ownership after new towns are founded; outlying homes explicitly retain null. Housing creation and demolition share `housingCapacity`. A finished construction gesture refreshes network connections while paused.

`monthlyOperatingExpenses` separates upkeep from total cash expenditure. Routes accumulate allocated vehicle/station/network expenses; shared infrastructure is charged once, with unassigned infrastructure and factories left as company overhead. Legacy saves establish revenue baselines and accounting start days so historical fares are not compared with nonexistent historical upkeep. New worlds and loaded saves both write the next autosave before replacing the active game.

## Square-world persistence and material detail

`transport-procedural-v1` retains the generation descriptor and packed changed tiles. `rememberGeneratedWorld` stores an exact four-byte baseline per tile plus sparse extras in a WeakMap, using 16 MiB for 2048² without retaining a second object grid. Every save compares current fields with that baseline, preserving direct edits, unknown properties, nested fields and deletion/reversion. Changed indices use delta varints and existing UTF16 tile packing. Loading regenerates the explicitly versioned recipe, captures its baseline and applies patches. Legacy JSON and compact-v1 saves continue to decode. Metadata listing validates packed fields without regenerating a second continent.

`water-art.js` paints cached depth/bank detail in the water clip; small live ripples derive from simulation day. `raster-houses.js` supplies nine generated house designs per biome, with 256×256 transparent masters and prefiltered 16/32/64/128-pixel sprite cells. The runtime loads only the smaller atlases, choosing a cell size matching `32 × zoom × devicePixelRatio`. Artwork occupies a 32×32 square within the existing 32×40 sprite envelope. `lighting.js` uses hand-measured pane rectangles for each house and biome.

Startup waits at most four seconds for house and world artwork, loading both groups concurrently. Each decoded density becomes available independently; a missing resolution uses another loaded resolution of the same artwork. Late arrivals increment a separate artwork revision, refreshing sprite/chunk caches and interface thumbnails without changing game state. Missing biome artwork can use the same identity from another available climate, with matching window anchors; native drawings remain the final fallback when no image is usable. Connectivity recovery retries only missing densities. `worldArtStats()` reports usable atlases, failures and actual generated-image draws by identity. Asset loading, downscaling provenance and prompts are documented in `assets/houses/README.md`. `processing-sprites.js` retains native factory/extractor fallback drawings; production rules remain in the economy catalog.

`index.html` includes a visible full-screen loading dialog and an inert game shell. The lightweight `boot.js` promotes that dialog to the native top layer and paints before importing `app.js`; import/startup failures keep a retry action available. `loading-screen.js` reports three actual preparation stages, with live status text and reduced-motion support. Startup, new-world creation and named-save reading paint the loader before expensive synchronous work, then render the map and minimap before revealing the game. Loading blocks gameplay shortcuts, simulation frames and background autosaves. Recoverable save/generation failures close the loader in `finally` and return to the original dialog. `tests/loading-screen-browser-check.mjs` exercises delayed and failed imports, local-save loading, storage failure/retry and mobile reduced motion in isolated storage.

`world-v2.js` combines the terrain and placement recipes in `world-terrain-v2.js` and `world-placement-v2.js`. Recipes through version 6 retain their original geography: recipe 4 preserves underlying elevation beneath roads and settlements, recipe 5 allocates full building and industry plots, and recipe 6 adds level multi-tile terrain objects. The starter dry-land area blends into its surroundings. This avoids rectangular trenches around settlements. New square worlds use recipe 7: `world-mountains-v7.js` adds seeded local peaks, short asymmetric ridges and desert mesas to the saved elevation field before settlement placement. High ground between features becomes broad valleys; water and the protected opening corridor keep their original elevations. Peaks reach the visual level-7 ceiling without a second world-sized height array. `world.js` retains recipes 1–6 and the old rectangular sizes, with frozen digest fixtures. Shared deterministic primitives live in `world-noise.js`. The save descriptor, baseline and validation carry the explicit generation version, so old companies regenerate their original geography. Never change a released recipe without introducing a new version and retaining existing digest fixtures.

## Interface artwork

`ui-art.js` renders the generated sprite identities into build menus, industry lists and inspectors, station inspectors, production-chain nodes and route/purchase vehicle portraits. Canvas backing density follows DPR up to 2, with smooth downsampling; a cache key includes biome, vehicle type/generation and both artwork revisions. Dynamic filtering, cargo/mode selection, upgrades and late asset arrivals redraw affected portraits. New-world previews also use DPR-sized canvases. An online event retries missing world/house atlas densities without changing company state. Resource and action icons remain semantic SVG pictograms. `tests/ui-art-browser-check.mjs` exercises these paths on desktop and mobile, including list replacement and Retina rendering.

## Generated world artwork and industry sites

`atlas-runtime.js` loads prefiltered display atlases and publishes usable densities independently, selects a level for the actual render density, and notifies sprite, chunk, marine and palette caches when artwork arrives. It never mutates simulation state. `raster-buildings.js`, `raster-industries.js`, `raster-nature.js` and `raster-transport.js` share that registry and retain native fallback drawings. Original sources and prompt records are documented in `assets/world/README.md`.

`industry-sites.js` owns footprint geometry and validation. New industries use `footprint: 2`; absent or explicit `footprint: 1` preserves legacy extent. Every occupied tile resolves to the same industry for picking, demolition and overlap prevention. Station catchment uses the nearest site tile; environment access, production conditions and service-related upkeep sample the whole site. Industry artwork uses a 64×72 logical canvas for a two-tile site, with measured window anchors scaled accordingly.

`vehicle-directions.js` selects one of eight independently drawn frames for each of nine vehicle identities from `vehicle-{kind}-dimetric-v2/`. Canvas angles start east and increase clockwise. Artwork stays in the fixed world camera while loads, route-color markings and lights follow the quantized heading. Each trailing train car uses its own path segment angle. Marine caches include heading and load band; art revisions invalidate their frames. Packing applies one shared scale across the sheet, preserving north/south foreshortening. `projectedGroundBasis()` projects overhead cargo patches exactly once onto the ground plane; body sprites and the southeast fallback remain upright.

## Continuous terrain relief

`terrain-elevation.js` reads the precise saved `tile.elevation` on a 0–16 scale; water is level zero. This legacy scale remains the source representation for old procedural recipes and save metadata; player-facing heights use eight discrete vertex levels. Rendering does not mutate terrain or add a second saved height field. A nonnegative cubic B-spline over neighboring tile centers blends heights, biome ground colors and geological coverage into a continuous surface. The overview retains analytical gradient lighting. The isometric mesh requests `terrainReliefRaster(..., {lighting:false})` (fourth parameter), retaining the blended texture colors while applying lighting from the actual geometric faces.

Ground is sampled at six points per tile into a reusable small canvas, then smoothly drawn into the existing bounded chunk cache. Sampling phases, soil moisture, fine grain and geological texture are world-aligned, producing byte-identical shared samples in overlapping chunks. Two-tile fingerprint padding covers the spline support, and fingerprints include fractional elevation. Forest density follows neighboring woodland and regional noise. Single-tile rock density is reduced to 18% of its former selection rate; large rock parcels retain their visible footprints. Mountain sprites are suppressed, with their geological texture retained on the raised ground. The overview uses the same altitude colors and a cheaper slope estimate. A material field combines world-aligned moisture patches, fine grass/sand grain and restrained geological variation. The renderer avoids repeated per-tile sand arcs and pale washes that would obscure that material. `landscape-scenery.js` selects presentation-only patches of local flowers and grasses, keeping scattered detail stones rare without rewriting saved ecology. Habitat patches mix species instead of repeating lichen everywhere; empty detail stays bare after bulldozing or earthworks. `tests/terrain-elevation.test.mjs` verifies interpolation and seams; `tests/terrain-elevation-browser-check.mjs` covers live elevation edits across chunks, exact restoration, all environments, zooms and display densities.

`shoreline.js` traces water boundaries, filters neighboring contour controls and adds subtle world-aligned bank variation. The resulting curves replace repeated rounded tile corners while preserving land/water tile centers, isolated ponds and narrow channels. Padded chunks produce identical shared curves; `water-art.js` adds local shallows and damp banks without a uniform bright outline. Its coast pass follows the same smoothed contours, ignores artificial chunk edges, and clips translucent shelves and broken foam to water. Animation uses a sparse seed-based selection at every zoom and simulation time, so Pause freezes the exact frame; moving ripples never rebuild terrain chunks. `tests/shoreline.test.mjs` checks navigation clearance and seams. `tests/landscape-realism-browser-check.mjs` captures deterministic town, forest, highland and coast scenes across environments, zooms and display densities, and checks canopy clipping and cache limits in isolated browser storage.

## Raised isometric geometry

`terrain-geometry.js` maps source elevation to eight integer vertex heights, 0–7, with 24 projected pixels per height step. The legacy 0–16 source helpers and structure metadata remain unchanged. An exact Chebyshev lower envelope limits all eight neighboring vertices to one level of difference, using an eight-point halo; a 96-entry LRU caches 32×32 vertex chunks without a whole-world height array. Each tile has two triangles split along NW–SE. Shared corner points touching water are at sea level. The diagonal bound prevents folded faces even on the taller slopes. Centers interpolate from NW and SE; they are not independent height samples. `surfaceHeight`, `projectGround` and `pickGround` use the same planes for rendering, pointer selection and overlays.

`terrain-mesh.js` warps the existing authored ground and network textures onto those triangles. Each face uses orientation-dependent surface-normal lighting, with antialiased joins tested at every supported raster scale. Each visible 6×6 terrain chunk caches only its projected mesh against the existing memory budget. One reusable source-texture canvas serves every chunk, avoiding redundant Retina bitmaps and eviction churn without reducing texture resolution. The geometry halo participates in chunk fingerprints, so nearby height edits refresh every affected slope. Large-map minimaps retain bounded sampling.

Camera focus, panning and anchored zoom use the raised projection. Ground grids and construction previews follow the mesh. Buildings sit on foundations at the highest center or corner in their complete footprint, with retaining faces where necessary. Bridge decks resolve a constant span height from their displayed bank levels; network-only shore textures ramp to that deck at the shared edge, and vehicle positions follow the same approach. Lighting receives separate building, ground and transport projection callbacks. None of these view transforms alter saved elevation, networks or routes.

## Terrain construction controls

`app.js` groups earthworks and explicit crossings in the expandable Network → Terrain & crossings panel. Raise/lower gestures use the same deduplicated construction plan, prices, notifications, revision handling and autosave path as other tools. Terrain tools snap to visible grid vertices and mark their connecting edges. Each raise/lower drag captures every selected point’s target before mutation, verifies the final limited surface, and commits the complete stroke atomically. A point already moved by a neighboring edit is not lowered twice. Quotes and previews use the same plan. Level area uses a rectangle anchored at its first point’s displayed integer height. `planTerraformLevel`, `quoteTerraformLevel` and `buildTerraformLevel` preflight the complete area and funds before charging per changed height step. A point already displayed at the requested height is a free no-op, even when its legacy source is fractional. Raises and leveling boundaries reject heights the limiter cannot display; edited sources save as level/7 through the existing codec. Adjoining water and occupied cells protect their shared corners. A bounded counterfactual also rejects edits whose slope influence would move more distant occupied corners. Bridge/tunnel gestures snap to one horizontal or vertical axis; the shared plan quote provides level, total price and validation feedback. Road/rail selection changes the explicit crossing mode without adding four permanent toolbar buttons.

Span validation and atomic construction belong to the model and construction planner, so previews and committed spans share the same geometry and constraints. New crossings require flat endpoint cells at matching displayed heights. Interior bridge faces stay at or below the deck with clearance, and tunnel faces stay at or above the bore with cover. Legacy raw-height validation remains available for saved crossings; new source-clipped banks use the geometric envelope. The renderer uses the existing saved elevation for terrain and span metadata for level crossings. `tests/earthworks-browser-check.mjs` exercises the controls through browser pointer events and isolated local storage.

`terrain-engineering.js` centralizes earthwork protection, span geometry and network edge validation. New ordinary networks use the rendered four-corner surface: near-flat ground accepts junctions, while monotonic straight inclines permit only their uphill axis. Side slopes, corner slopes, crowns and turning/joining a ramp sideways reject the complete stroke before payment. Existing saved networks remain traversable. Interior span tiles store `structureLevel` and `structureAxis`; approaches remain ordinary network tiles. Pathfinding permits entry along the span axis at its deck or bore level, while legacy untagged networks retain their original connection rules. Construction invalidates route caches once, demolition removes the metadata, and the existing sparse save codec preserves both elevation edits and span fields without a format migration. `structure-visibility.js` shares underground vehicle visibility between the renderer and night lighting. Model tests cover atomic failures, routing, repairs and saved-world restoration; the engineering renderer check verifies portals, underground vehicles, previews and cache limits at all three zooms.
# Large-world performance

Measured on the development machine in Node and headless Chrome in September 2026. These are regression workloads, not a promised frame rate on every device. The map-size limit remains **2048 × 2048**.

## Changes

- The app redraws only when the company, camera, selection, artwork, or map controls change. Pause stops water/weather/light animation and idle map repainting. Hidden tabs do not simulate. A hidden minimap and closed management panels do no recurring drawing or list rebuilding.
- Terrain height fields use bounded byte caches with numeric keys. Cached mesh canvases contain their actual projected bounds instead of allocating empty maximum-height margins. Static scenery and grid paths are reused.
- Route drawing indexes ordered segment runs by spatial cell. Only the visible sections are projected; the minimap reuses complete route paths. Distant vehicles and their lights do not query terrain heights.
- A shared network bitset costs 512 KiB at 2048², even when every tile carries a network. Construction updates it incrementally. Ecology does not trigger a full network scan.
- Vehicle arrivals use a time-ordered event queue instead of rescanning the fleet for every arrival. Spatial buckets bound nearby settlement, industry, zone and station queries. Fleet and station lookup tables replace repeated array scans. Local routes retain breadth-first search; distant routes use shortest-path A* and can choose a different equally short route.
- Generated tile elevations share immutable exact numbers while tiles remain independently mutable ordinary objects. Artwork loads for the active climate; authored building sprites reuse identical canvases across legacy variant numbers.
- Saves preserve generated terrain as lossless baseline deltas. Repeated network changes compress into runs. Long cardinal routes use exact direction runs rather than repeated coordinate objects. Large fleets share record field names and store fractional values as exact IEEE754 bits. Legacy saves remain readable.
- Route search applies to the whole fleet, while the UI shows 50 cards per page. It does not create thousands of canvases and DOM cards at once.

## Representative measurements

| Workload | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Paused app, 3 seconds, map redraws | 181 | 0 |
| Paused app, 3 seconds, script time | 1,360 ms | about 5 ms |
| Decoded world atlases, initial taiga world | 60.2 MiB | 33.7 MiB |
| Real 2048² generated tile heap | 519.4 MiB | 455.5 MiB |
| Forest/coast, Detail at DPR 2, warm renderer | 52–53 ms | about 6–8 ms |
| 2048², 10,000 vehicles, 1,000 short routes, 120 simulation steps | 48.35 s | 1.27 s |
| Cross-map shortest-path search | about 630 ms | about 10 ms |
| Road/rail grid every 8 tiles, 2048² terrain save | 5.53 MiB | 0.99 MiB |
| Route panel with 10,000 routes | formerly unbounded cards | 50 cards, about 25–55 ms opening |

The fleet benchmark flattens **4,194,304 independently mutable tiles** into a synthetic connected network, connecting stops near every existing town and industry. Its short journeys deliberately create frequent arrivals. It bypasses construction costs and terrain constraints to isolate simulation scaling; it does not claim every synthetic route is a commercially valid passenger service. Long-distance route finding is measured separately. Daily updates still produce occasional spikes.

The renderer benchmark uses a synthetic connected grid of 983,040 road/rail tiles, 1,000 routes representing 2,047,000 logical segments, and 10,000 vehicles, with 41–90 intentionally visible at each zoom. It shares immutable terrain fixtures to isolate rendering rather than measuring world memory. Warm views recompose no terrain and rebuild no route paths. A pan considers fewer than 0.8% of the route segments. Cold minimap creation is roughly 220–250 ms; warm reuse is roughly 1 ms.

A separate save test mutates over four million tiles in a real generated 2048² world. Its terrain-heavy autosave is about 2.02 MiB and restores every tile exactly. A combined stress fixture with 4.19 million network flags, 1,000 routes of 4,075 points, and 10,000 vehicles with fractional positions uses **4.19 MiB** (including all route and fleet state) and round-trips tiles, route points and vehicles exactly. Encoding took 1.79 seconds and decoding took 5.78 seconds in that run. Arbitrary new tile fields and unusual precision are retained with a lossless fallback rather than silently rounded.

## Practical limits

A raw 4096² generation probe used about **1.8 GiB of JavaScript heap**, before renderer surfaces, path buffers, fleets, save reconstruction or browser overhead. It is not exposed as a playable size. Larger supported maps require a packed/lazy tile representation and a save strategy that avoids retaining both worlds while replacing one.

Normal menu generation/restoration and live save encoding now use background workers (measurements below). Page-leave checkpoints, compatibility callers and worker-unavailable fallbacks still perform synchronous validation/terrain scans. A fully modified 2048² synchronous save can take roughly 1.3–1.8 seconds; loading while keeping the previous company for failure recovery can briefly double world memory. Fully paused unchanged worlds skip periodic autosave scans. Long-network edits can still require multiple route replans, and worst-case winding routes do not compress as well as straight lines. Local-storage quota is shared by all named saves and depends on the browser.

## Reproduce

Run from the repository root with its static server serving port 8765. Set `TRANSPORT_PLAYWRIGHT` to the installed Playwright module if it is not available as `playwright`.

```sh
node --test --test-concurrency=2 fun/transport/tests/*.test.mjs
node --expose-gc --max-old-space-size=2048 fun/transport/tests/dense-world-benchmark.mjs
node --expose-gc --max-old-space-size=4096 fun/transport/tests/dense-save-benchmark.mjs --roundtrip
node fun/transport/tests/rendering-performance-browser-check.mjs
node fun/transport/tests/app-performance-browser-check.mjs
node fun/transport/tests/start-menu-browser-check.mjs
node fun/transport/tests/compact-play-browser-check.mjs
node fun/transport/tests/weather-effects-browser-check.mjs
node fun/transport/tests/loading-screen-browser-check.mjs
```

The browser checks use isolated storage and never edit the player's saved companies. Timing values are reported; correctness, cache bounds, conservation, exact save restoration, idle invalidation, and visible interactions are asserted.

## Busy-screen rendering

A second pass profiles what is actually on screen: dense woodland, a large city, and crowded roads and railways. Its baseline is the completed large-world work above, before the additional sprite, lighting and scene-cache changes.

Nature, buildings and transport now use shared, bounded prepared-image caches across the three zoom levels. The artwork is rendered at the required physical-pixel size; revisiting a prepared zoom does not resize every instance again. The static artwork pool is capped at 128 MiB, transport at 32 MiB, and tree shadows at 32 MiB. Larger visible groves previously exhausted the 16 MiB sprite cache and could recreate thousands of identical images every frame. In one 24-frame Detail woodland run, the old renderer created 10,632 sprites; the new renderer created none after warming.

Small camera moves reuse scenery ordering and foundation geometry. Moving vehicles are merged into that order, preserving occlusion. Exact sprite and shadow rectangles reject objects outside the screen; shadow smoothing state is set once for the batch. Night lighting uses cached emitter descriptions, window artwork and directional headlight beams. Cargo badges reuse prepared artwork while preserving their load indicators.

The full suite covers **54 views**: six scenes × three zooms × daylight, night and rain, at 1280 × 900 CSS pixels and DPR 2. It includes a real 512² taiga world (seed 418), its densest sampled forest and largest town, plus staged flat landscapes. The staged city contains 21,139 buildings and 157 industries. The fleet contains 3,102 vehicles; Region considers 1,257 nearby vehicles and paints roughly 1,041 visible load badges. Detail still paints 63 visible badges. These are rendering fixtures, without construction costs or an economic simulation step in the measured interval.

Warm frame and pan values below are medians in milliseconds. The first three rows are a separate paired forest run in fresh browser contexts, with 24 warm frames and 24 pan steps. Remaining rows come from the complete 54-view sequence, with 12 frames per phase. That sequence retains multiple scene fixtures and exercises a larger graphics working set. Pixel hashes use a separate readback canvas so verification does not switch the game's primary canvas toward frequent-readback rendering.

| View | Warm before → after | Panning before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Dense woodland, Region | 17.3 → 11.4 ms | 25.0 → 15.0 ms |
| Dense woodland, Town | 6.5 → 4.6 ms | 8.7 → 5.6 ms |
| Dense woodland, Detail | 42.1 → 2.1 ms | 41.7 → 2.4 ms |
| Generated dense forest, Town, daylight | 90.6 → 5.4 ms | 67.6 → 7.7 ms |
| Large city, Region, night | 19.3 → 7.7 ms | 27.1 → 10.7 ms |
| Crowded fleet, Region, daylight | 12.8 → 5.5 ms | 22.0 → 11.9 ms |
| Large city + crowded fleet, Region, night | 45.5 → 14.6 ms | 58.8 → 19.6 ms |

All 54 updated warm views created **zero nature, building, vehicle or shadow images**, rebuilt no static scenes, and recomposed no terrain chunks. Panning can populate newly exposed terrain and rebuild the scenery border periodically. All three zooms retain the same objects and artwork. The full sequence's dense woodland Region daylight result was 12.9 ms warm / 17.1 ms panning, compared with 20.5 / 31.6 ms before; the separate fresh-context row above is reported independently.

Render-call duration is not the displayed frame interval. In the paired Detail woodland run, the median animation-frame interval fell from 171.7 to 16.7 ms. The combined city/fleet night scene fell from 48.9 to 22.9 ms; its remaining draw/compositing work still exceeds a 60 Hz frame budget. Cold views, system load and retained graphics surfaces also affect results. These measurements do not promise 60 fps or remove simulation/save costs.

A separate **100-case** browser regression compares a reused renderer with a newly created one after small, long and reverse pans, visibility toggles, terrain/building revisions, zoom changes and late artwork loading. Every visible RGBA pixel and sampled inspection target matches. Before/after daytime Town screenshots of forests and buildings also match exactly. Prepared vehicle/badge edges and cached night lights have small rasterization differences; all directions, load states and footprints receive independent artwork checks.

```sh
# Full sequence; warm caches must not rerasterize visible objects.
TRANSPORT_EXPECT_STABLE_SPRITES=1 node fun/transport/tests/busy-scenes-browser-check.mjs

# Independent forest run, with a fresh browser context for each selected scene.
TRANSPORT_FRESH_SCENES=1 TRANSPORT_SCENES=forest TRANSPORT_CONDITIONS=day TRANSPORT_FRAMES=24 \
  TRANSPORT_EXPECT_STABLE_SPRITES=1 node fun/transport/tests/busy-scenes-browser-check.mjs

# Cached/fresh frame and inspection equivalence, including invalidations.
node fun/transport/tests/scene-cache-browser-check.mjs
```

`TRANSPORT_URL` selects an immutable comparison server, `TRANSPORT_OUTPUT` selects the results/screenshot directory, and `TRANSPORT_PROFILE=1` records Chrome CPU profiles for Region daylight/night views. Timings are reported rather than asserted against device-specific thresholds.

## Background world and save jobs

New-world generation, restore/migration, validation and save encoding run in module workers. The main thread receives transferable terrain/route buffers and materializes ordinary game objects in yielding slices. Existing save formats and exact procedural baselines are preserved. The menu loading view stays responsive and supports cancellation before activation. Autosaves coalesce repeated requests and reject results belonging to cancelled or replaced companies; named save writes retain their single atomic local-storage commit.

The worker benchmark uses a real generated taiga map (seed 1847), verifies byte-identical generated and edited saves against the synchronous model, restores an edited building, and cancels an in-flight creation. A 16 ms UI heartbeat records the longest main-thread gap. These figures cover the worker/capture/hydration operation, not subsequent artwork loading or first terrain rendering.

| Map and operation | Synchronous maximum UI gap | Background maximum UI gap |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1024² generation | 361 ms | 26 ms |
| 1024² restore | 483 ms | 28 ms |
| 1024² save validation/encoding | 226 ms | 23 ms capture / 17 ms encoding |
| 2048² generation | 1,137 ms | 47 ms |
| 2048² restore | 1,746 ms | 34 ms |
| 2048² save validation/encoding | 897 ms | 24 ms capture / 22 ms encoding |

This improves responsiveness, not total throughput. Including the benchmark's final 25 ms heartbeat window, 2048² generation took 1.16 seconds synchronously and 2.44 seconds with transfer/hydration; restoration took 1.77 and 2.87 seconds. Consistent capture held simulation for approximately 0.72 seconds on that map while allowing the UI to respond; play resumed during approximately 0.97 seconds of worker encoding. Snapshot capture and materialization still allocate memory, and a very large fleet or heavily extended tile state can increase their cost. Route planning remains synchronous. Page-leave checkpoints and unsupported-worker fallbacks also retain synchronous behavior.

Browser regression checks cover startup, cancellation by button/Escape, save-slot round trips, quotas, delayed stale worker responses, overlapping saves, continued simulation during encoding and the final page-leave checkpoint. The new UI scenarios pass on both 512² and 2048² maps. All 417 model tests pass.

```sh
node fun/transport/tests/background-jobs-browser-check.mjs
REDACTED node fun/transport/tests/background-jobs-browser-check.mjs
node fun/transport/tests/background-ui-browser-check.mjs
REDACTED node fun/transport/tests/background-ui-browser-check.mjs
```

## Scenery batches after native sprite preparation

A further pass batches static sprites on narrow depth diagonals and caches the tree-shadow ground layer. Vehicle ordering remains exact: a vehicle inside a strip's ordering range causes that strip to draw its original objects. Original sprite masks still drive inspection. Bridges, stations and tunnel mouths remain independent. The extra batch/shadow pool is capped at **96 MiB**, and oversized views fall back to direct drawing.

Preparation has a roughly **3 ms** per-frame budget; a shadow layer becomes visible only when complete. Continuous camera movement suspends preparation until the camera has settled for 90 ms. Original sprites remain visible throughout. This avoids spending time rebuilding caches that another pan would immediately discard. The first prototype improved median panning but doubled dense-forest pan P90 to about 48 ms; staged, camera-aware preparation removes that rebuild spike. Continuous-pan regression checks record zero raster-preparation time.

This comparison uses an immutable copy of the completed native-sprite work, fresh browser contexts per scene, 1280 × 900 CSS pixels, DPR 2, 24 warm frames and 24 pan steps. The harness waits for pending preparation before measuring warm frames. Warm and pan values are medians in milliseconds:

| View | Warm before → after | Panning before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Dense woodland, Region, daylight | 10.8 → 2.7 ms | 14.4 → 14.7 ms |
| Dense woodland, Town, daylight | 4.3 → 1.9 ms | 5.3 → 5.1 ms |
| Dense woodland, Detail, daylight | 2.1 → 1.5 ms | 2.5 → 1.6 ms |
| City + crowded fleet, Region, daylight | 7.9 → 7.0 ms | 14.1 → 14.1 ms |
| City + crowded fleet, Region, night | 12.9 → 12.4 ms | 18.4 → 18.7 ms |

The gain is strongest in stationary woodland views; crowded fleets still require individual moving-vehicle, cargo and light draws. Continuous Region panning remains approximately at the preceding implementation's cost: forest daylight P90 was 22.7 → 24.4 ms. Batch warming cannot remove terrain's first-render cost. These results do not imply a general 60 fps guarantee.

Paired batched/direct image checks cover moving vehicles, panning beyond the cached border, terrain edits, visibility changes, all three zooms, fractional display density and Retina. Transitional checks also compare partially prepared frames and verify queues finish after the camera settles. Picking is identical; small channel differences from transparent compositing are bounded separately from geometry. Warm rendering creates no new nature, building, vehicle or shadow sprites. The separate 100-case cached/fresh-view regression now waits for staged preparation and allows at most four channel levels of transparency roundoff with a mean difference ≤0.02/255; inspection targets still match exactly.

```sh
node fun/transport/tests/scenery-batches-browser-check.mjs
TRANSPORT_FRESH_SCENES=1 TRANSPORT_SCENES=forest,mixed TRANSPORT_CONDITIONS=day,night \
  TRANSPORT_FRAMES=24 TRANSPORT_EXPECT_STABLE_SPRITES=1 \
  node fun/transport/tests/busy-scenes-browser-check.mjs
```

name: ashline-dev-workflow
description: "How to serve, test, and screenshot fun/ashline in this environment (Playwright path, sandbox caveat, RNG-pinning tests that constrain terrain changes)"

Ashline (fun/ashline) dev loop, verified 2026-09-06:

- Serve from the repo root: `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory /Users/vojta/Dev/protocodus.github.io`; the game is at http://127.0.0.1:8000/fun/ashline/. Starting the server from inside fun/ashline gives 404s.
- Node sim checks: `cd fun/ashline && node tests/<name>-check.mjs` (sim, orders, explore, production, processing, rocket, rank, collision, formation, path-smoothing, building-actions, lava, distribution, save). All pass on main as of da1c7b4. macOS has no `timeout` binary.
- Browser checks need `REDACTED.mjs` and the `chrome` channel. Three of them (faction-browser, rank-browser, trees-browser) default to port 8131, so always pass `ASHLINE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000/fun/ashline/`. Chrome cannot launch inside the Bash sandbox (crashpad bootstrap "Permission denied", ProcessSingleton errors); run Playwright commands with the sandbox disabled. `pkill`/`lsof` also fail sandboxed.
- Screenshots via Read work well for judging terrain; set `s.fogClock = 1e9` before filling `visible[0]`/`explored[0]` or the next sim tick re-fogs the map.
- Terrain generator changes are pinned by tests: tests/lava-check.mjs asserts exact post-generation `s.rng` values for legacy 72x56 seeds (ASH-001, smoke, player-victory) and tests/distribution-check.mjs asserts mineral budgets within 3% for the same seeds. Any change to the number of gameplay `random(s)` draws in generateMap requires re-recording those constants; use hashed side streams (`hash(seed+':name')`) for new terrain features to avoid touching gameplay RNG.

**Why:** the sandbox and RNG-pinning facts cost real time to rediscover.
**How to apply:** follow the commands above; when changing generation, decide up front whether to preserve the `random(s)` draw sequence or re-record the pinned constants. See also [[alpen-debug-workflow]].

Tyran (fun/tyran), verified 2026-09-25 after the Galaga/Tyrian redesign (waves.js director, power, drones, captor, novas, reserve ships, challenging stages):

- Port 8773 (the README default) was already held by another process and returned empty responses; serve the repo root with a `Cache-Control: no-store` handler on a fresh port (e.g. 8791) and pass `TYRAN_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8791/fun/tyran/`. Browser checks also need `REDACTED.mjs` and must run with the sandbox disabled (see [[ashline-dev-workflow]]). `TYRAN_SCREENSHOTS` defaults to $TMPDIR/tyran-qa, which resolves under /var/folders when unsandboxed.
- Node suites: `node tests/sim-check.mjs [--balance]`, `save-game-check`, `ground-combat-check`, `tile-map-check`. Any test that wants a quiet arena must set `state.director.hold = true` (or `bossSpawned = true`); the old `spawnTimer/showcase = Infinity` trick no longer stops spawns. Tests that expect instant defeat must set `state.lives = 0`. Sector 1/3/5/7/9 guardians lead into a challenging stage before the shop; browser tests skip it by marking `enemy.challenge` ships `gone` and stepping ~5 s.
- `window.tyran.step()` advances the sim but not effects; for fast-forward screenshots also call `tyran.fx.update(dt)` (QA hatch) or smoke piles up and screenshots look cluttered. Hide `#announcement` before shots — its timer uses the rAF clock, not step().
- Balance: `--balance` bot must win; a pilot that only holds fire must lose ships in sector 1 and be defeated within three sectors. Original game earned ~3.6k–5.9k credits/sector; the redesign targets ~1.5× that because the shop gained guns, drones, novas and reserve ships.

- Performance (2026-09-25): steady flight is cheap (render ≈1 ms, sim ≈0.2 ms/frame even at 4× CPU throttle); hitches come from synchronous GPU readbacks — drawing a GPU-backed canvas into a `willReadFrequently` canvas, or `getImageData` on a GPU canvas, can stall 10–100 ms. Atlases that are only recolored are now CPU-resident (`CPU_ATLASES` in sprite-assets.js); keep new pixel-reading code on CPU scratches. `tests/stutter-check.mjs` guards this, the hitstop freeze and the shop's next-sector prewarm. To find stalls: wrap `CanvasRenderingContext2D/OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D.prototype.getImageData` with timing + stack, wrap `Object.getPrototypeOf(tyran.world)` methods (getTile/getSceneryLayer/getSprite) to attribute long rAF frames, and reconstruct contiguous busy segments from a CDP Profiler sample timeline. Playwright's own result serialization shows up as ~250 ms `serialize/innerSerialize` segments — ignore them. Pages with mocked rAF need `waitForFunction(..., { polling: 50 })`, since the default polls on rAF.

**Why:** these facts cost real time to rediscover (occupied port, fx not aging in step(), director ignoring the old spawn-timer switches).
**How to apply:** start from these commands; when changing difficulty or economy, rerun `--balance` and compare per-sector `earned`.

name: alpen-debug-workflow
description: "How to run, drive and verify the Alpen snowboarding game (fun/alpen) in a headless browser session"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 122db08e-5f2c-4b4f-b5dd-8cbf6a8d18f1
  modified: 2026-09-24T20:28:58.080Z
---

Alpen (fun/alpen) must be served from the **repo root** (protocodus.github.io), not the game dir — index.html imports three.js via the absolute path `/assets/vendor/three/three.module.min.js`. `python3 -m http.server <port>` from the root works. Vendored three is r185; GLTFLoader + utils live under fun/alpen/assets/vendor|utils.

Verification hatches (as of 2026-08-07):
- `?seed=<code>` pins the mountain; the game writes the generated seed back into the URL.
- `window.__alpen.debug()` returns a full state snapshot; `__alpen.rider/game/scene/...` expose live objects. `debug().speed` is roughly HUD km/h × 4.35.
- `__alpen.weather.pin(tod)` freezes time-of-day (~0.35 bright morning, 0.6–0.7 golden hour, 0.93+ aurora); conditions are NOT tod-driven — loop `__alpen.weather.update(10)` until `state.storm` is where you want it. Storms rebuild over time, re-clear before beauty shots.
- Drive by dispatching KeyboardEvents on `window` (Enter starts; A/D carve, W tuck, S brake, Space pop, R restart-at-last-gate, Escape pause). **Always send matching keyup** — a keydown-only S latches the brake at 1 and the rider stands still forever.
- Probing terrain: `import('/fun/alpen/js/terrain.js')` in-page gives `guideAt(z)` (racing-line x), `gateSlotsIn(zLo,zHi)`, `rockBandAt(z)` (zone widths), `getTerrainMaterialAt(x,z)` ({groomed,powder,rock,ice}), `corridorHalfAt`, `nearestCenter`. Downhill is **−z**.
- **Never mutate `rider.pos`/`vel` from evaluate scripts** — the render half of `frame()` swaps pos/yaw for interpolation and restores them, so external writes race and corrupt state (rider flung at 200+). Use the R-restart path instead; spawns snap to `guideAt`.
- **Zero-input drift is a real regression signal, not noise — test it, don't wave it off.** Protocol: reset, send zero input, sample `pos` + `corridorHalfAt`/`nearestCenter` from terrain.js once or twice a second for 25-30s. Do this after any change to `TERRAIN.corridor`/`TERRAIN.guide`, the off-piste octave masking, **or any yaw rule in `groundStep`**.
  - **Judge the shape, not an absolute number.** A previous version of this memory claimed the fix of 2026-08-07 left drift at "single digits to low teens of metres over 30s". That was wrong — measured on 2026-08-07 across 5 seeds × 4 start points it was 80–156 m, and in the live browser too. Correct pass criterion: **bounded and oscillating** (offset crosses back through zero, yaw stays within a few degrees) rather than **monotonic** (offset and yaw grow together without ever turning back). A passive rider legitimately ends tens of metres off-centre because the piste's own centre line wanders away from anyone riding straight; that is not the bug. Yaw sweeping 0°→67° with no input is.
  - The real cause found on 2026-08-07 was **not** terrain: the self-centring rule in `rider.js` compared `atan2(vel.x,-vel.z)` (world horizontal bearing) against `this.yaw`, while the velocity is rebuilt along `h` — the heading *projected onto the slope*, which has a different bearing on any cross-slope. The rule read that projection as steering error and removed it, enlarging it: positive feedback at up to 11°/s. Fixed by using `atan2(vLat, vFwd)` (the slip angle, in the board's own tangent frame). Beware this class generally — **any rule comparing raw `yaw` against a world-space travel bearing has the same latent bug**; the clamps (`limitCourseYaw`, the skid clamp) only avoid it because they are thresholds, not followers.
- Fork-closing zones (two branches converging back to one) are the one case this drift check doesn't cleanly promise — a passive rider can pick up real excursion there since the "correct" line itself sweeps fast. Observed self-correcting rather than diverging; not worth over-tuning against since real players always steer.

**Prefer a headless Node harness over the browser for anything about physics, handling or input.** `rider.js`, `terrain.js`, `config.js`, `noise.js` and `shadow-cache.js` import nothing from three — `rider.js` needs only a `Vector3`, so a ~40-line shim (`set/copy/add/addScaledVector/multiplyScalar/dot/cross/normalize/length/lengthSq/lerp`) plus `world = {height: heightAt, surfaceAt: getTerrainMaterialAt, canStall, beyond: beyondLipAt, grip:1, surfaceDrag:1}` runs the real 120 Hz loop in node from a `.mjs` with absolute import paths. Verified 2026-08-07: `heightAt/guideAt/nearestCenter/corridorHalfAt` match the browser digit-for-digit, so the mountain is purely procedural and the harness is faithful. This turns a flaky 30-second browser observation into a deterministic sweep over seeds × start points in under a second, and lets you instrument the rider by `sed`-copying `rider.js` into scratch and patching probes in. `input.js` also runs in node with a tiny `window` EventTarget + `KeyboardEvent` shim, which is how the display-rate jump bug was pinned down. Use the browser only for what actually needs a GPU: rendering, materials, shaders, screenshots.

Browser harness: both the Chrome DevTools MCP browser and the Playwright MCP browser have died mid-session under long WebGL runs here ("Target closed" / target-page-closed) — neither is reliably stable for a long verification session. Expect to re-navigate and lose in-page state; keep test scripts short and self-contained (reset + sample + return) rather than relying on continuing a prior page's state across tool calls. Playwright screenshots land in `.playwright-mcp/` or the CWD — delete them before committing.

**What worked instead (2026-09-24): standalone Playwright `.mjs` scripts in the scratchpad**, run with `node` and `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` (Chrome can't launch sandboxed): `chromium.launch({ channel: 'chrome', headless: true, args: ['--use-angle=metal', '--enable-gpu', '--ignore-gpu-blocklist'] })` from `/Users/vojta/Dev/evangelist-exchange/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs` (see [[ashline-dev-workflow]]). One launch per scenario never died over dozens of runs, gets a real GPU, and `EXT_disjoint_timer_query` works, so `debug().performance.gpuMs` is live. Useful pieces: a steering autopilot dispatching A/D keydown/keyup from `setInterval` toward `guideAt(z-30)`; freezing with `__alpen.game.mode='paused'` then posing `__alpen.camera` and calling `shading.update(weather.state, camera, 0, NaN); retro.render(scene, camera)` for exact beauty shots; `__alpen.flicker.hideRelief/hideTerrain` or toggling `sky.group` children by name for layer A/Bs. For before/after perf: `git archive HEAD fun/alpen assets/vendor assets/images | tar -x -C $TMPDIR/alpen-base` and serve it on a second port; fixed camera pose + `freezeResolution`, alternate base/new runs — GPU p50 noise is ±0.5 ms on this machine, so single runs prove nothing.

**Beware stale ES-module caches** when files change on disk mid-session: a plain reload keeps old modules, and the Playwright MCP exposes no ignore-cache reload. The reliable dodge is to **start `python3 -m http.server` on a fresh port and navigate there** — a new origin has no cache. Symptom to watch for: `TypeError: <newFn> is not a function` spamming from `frame()` while the file on disk plainly has it. Verify with `curl -s localhost:<port>/fun/alpen/js/<file>.js | grep <marker>` before blaming the code.
- **The user's own browser hits this too.** `http.server` sends no Cache-Control, so Chrome heuristically caches modules whose Last-Modified is old (e.g. `props.js` untouched for weeks) and a normal reload mixes new and old files. On 2026-09-24 the user reported "remove the light posts" after they were already gone — they were seeing cached `props.js`. When handing the user a local URL, serve with a `Cache-Control: no-store` handler (a 10-line `SimpleHTTPRequestHandler` subclass) on a fresh port.

**Frame-by-frame capture of a jump:** Playwright's `page.clock.install()` mid-run hands rAF a timestamp from a different time base, so `frame()` sees a negative dt and a terrain lookup throws `RangeError: Invalid array length`. description: "How to run, drive and verify the Alpen snowboarding game (fun/alpen) in a headless browser session"
metadata:

---

Alpen (fun/alpen) must be served from the **repo root** (protocodus.github.io), not the game dir — index.html imports three.js via the absolute path `/assets/vendor/three/three.module.min.js`. `python3 -m http.server <port>` from the root works. Vendored three is r185; GLTFLoader + utils live under fun/alpen/assets/vendor|utils.

Verification hatches (as of 2026-08-07):
- `?seed=<code>` pins the mountain; the game writes the generated seed back into the URL.
- `window.__alpen.debug()` returns a full state snapshot; `__alpen.rider/game/scene/...` expose live objects. `debug().speed` is roughly HUD km/h × 4.35.
- `__alpen.weather.pin(tod)` freezes time-of-day (~0.35 bright morning, 0.6–0.7 golden hour, 0.93+ aurora); conditions are NOT tod-driven — loop `__alpen.weather.update(10)` until `state.storm` is where you want it. Storms rebuild over time, re-clear before beauty shots.
- Drive by dispatching KeyboardEvents on `window` (Enter starts; A/D carve, W tuck, S brake, Space pop, R restart-at-last-gate, Escape pause). **Always send matching keyup** — a keydown-only S latches the brake at 1 and the rider stands still forever.
- Probing terrain: `import('/fun/alpen/js/terrain.js')` in-page gives `guideAt(z)` (racing-line x), `gateSlotsIn(zLo,zHi)`, `rockBandAt(z)` (zone widths), `getTerrainMaterialAt(x,z)` ({groomed,powder,rock,ice}), `corridorHalfAt`, `nearestCenter`. Downhill is **−z**.
- **Never mutate `rider.pos`/`vel` from evaluate scripts** — the render half of `frame()` swaps pos/yaw for interpolation and restores them, so external writes race and corrupt state (rider flung at 200+). Use the R-restart path instead; spawns snap to `guideAt`.
- **Zero-input drift is a real regression signal, not noise — test it, don't wave it off.** Protocol: reset, send zero input, sample `pos` + `corridorHalfAt`/`nearestCenter` from terrain.js once or twice a second for 25-30s. Do this after any change to `TERRAIN.corridor`/`TERRAIN.guide`, the off-piste octave masking, **or any yaw rule in `groundStep`**.
  - **Judge the shape, not an absolute number.** A previous version of this memory claimed the fix of 2026-08-07 left drift at "single digits to low teens of metres over 30s". That was wrong — measured on 2026-08-07 across 5 seeds × 4 start points it was 80–156 m, and in the live browser too. Correct pass criterion: **bounded and oscillating** (offset crosses back through zero, yaw stays within a few degrees) rather than **monotonic** (offset and yaw grow together without ever turning back). A passive rider legitimately ends tens of metres off-centre because the piste's own centre line wanders away from anyone riding straight; that is not the bug. Yaw sweeping 0°→67° with no input is.
  - The real cause found on 2026-08-07 was **not** terrain: the self-centring rule in `rider.js` compared `atan2(vel.x,-vel.z)` (world horizontal bearing) against `this.yaw`, while the velocity is rebuilt along `h` — the heading *projected onto the slope*, which has a different bearing on any cross-slope. The rule read that projection as steering error and removed it, enlarging it: positive feedback at up to 11°/s. Fixed by using `atan2(vLat, vFwd)` (the slip angle, in the board's own tangent frame). Beware this class generally — **any rule comparing raw `yaw` against a world-space travel bearing has the same latent bug**; the clamps (`limitCourseYaw`, the skid clamp) only avoid it because they are thresholds, not followers.
- Fork-closing zones (two branches converging back to one) are the one case this drift check doesn't cleanly promise — a passive rider can pick up real excursion there since the "correct" line itself sweeps fast. Observed self-correcting rather than diverging; not worth over-tuning against since real players always steer.

**Prefer a headless Node harness over the browser for anything about physics, handling or input.** `rider.js`, `terrain.js`, `config.js`, `noise.js` and `shadow-cache.js` import nothing from three — `rider.js` needs only a `Vector3`, so a ~40-line shim (`set/copy/add/addScaledVector/multiplyScalar/dot/cross/normalize/length/lengthSq/lerp`) plus `world = {height: heightAt, surfaceAt: getTerrainMaterialAt, canStall, beyond: beyondLipAt, grip:1, surfaceDrag:1}` runs the real 120 Hz loop in node from a `.mjs` with absolute import paths. Verified 2026-08-07: `heightAt/guideAt/nearestCenter/corridorHalfAt` match the browser digit-for-digit, so the mountain is purely procedural and the harness is faithful. This turns a flaky 30-second browser observation into a deterministic sweep over seeds × start points in under a second, and lets you instrument the rider by `sed`-copying `rider.js` into scratch and patching probes in. `input.js` also runs in node with a tiny `window` EventTarget + `KeyboardEvent` shim, which is how the display-rate jump bug was pinned down. Use the browser only for what actually needs a GPU: rendering, materials, shaders, screenshots.

Browser harness: both the Chrome DevTools MCP browser and the Playwright MCP browser have died mid-session under long WebGL runs here ("Target closed" / target-page-closed) — neither is reliably stable for a long verification session. Expect to re-navigate and lose in-page state; keep test scripts short and self-contained (reset + sample + return) rather than relying on continuing a prior page's state across tool calls. Playwright screenshots land in `.playwright-mcp/` or the CWD — delete them before committing.

**What worked instead (2026-09-24): standalone Playwright `.mjs` scripts in the scratchpad**, run with `node` and `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` (Chrome can't launch sandboxed): `chromium.launch({ channel: 'chrome', headless: true, args: ['--use-angle=metal', '--enable-gpu', '--ignore-gpu-blocklist'] })` from `/Users/vojta/Dev/evangelist-exchange/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs` (see [[ashline-dev-workflow]]). One launch per scenario never died over dozens of runs, gets a real GPU, and `EXT_disjoint_timer_query` works, so `debug().performance.gpuMs` is live. Useful pieces: a steering autopilot dispatching A/D keydown/keyup from `setInterval` toward `guideAt(z-30)`; freezing with `__alpen.game.mode='paused'` then posing `__alpen.camera` and calling `shading.update(weather.state, camera, 0, NaN); retro.render(scene, camera)` for exact beauty shots; `__alpen.flicker.hideRelief/hideTerrain` or toggling `sky.group` children by name for layer A/Bs. **Beware stale ES-module caches** when files change on disk mid-session: a plain reload keeps old modules, and the Playwright MCP exposes no ignore-cache reload. The reliable dodge is to **start `python3 -m http.server` on a fresh port and navigate there** — a new origin has no cache. Verify with `curl -s localhost:<port>/fun/alpen/js/<file>.js | grep <marker>` before blaming the code.

The review is almost done. All 9 reviews and all 9 verification passes have finished, and the final step, turning the findings into an implementation plan, is running now. Nothing has been changed in the repo yet.

- **Proposals:** 84 across the 9 areas (8–10 each). The fact-checkers rejected none, but asked for corrections to most (71 corrected, 13 kept as written).
- **Ideas several reviewers raised on their own:**
  - Letting a route run more than one vehicle, since routes back up with cargo.
  - Road and rail drags that follow the terrain and show exactly where a slope blocks them.
  - Picking the cargo automatically in the route form.
  - Station and industry panels that link straight to route creation.
  - Map markers showing whether an industry is idle, starved of inputs or full.
  - Floating income over vehicles when they deliver.
  - A clearer queue for notifications.
  - Unique station names that you can rename.
  - A way to recover from debt instead of getting stuck.
  - A route health bug that shows up for industries larger than one tile (two reviewers found it independently).
- **Other notable proposals:**
  - A ladder of company milestones and cargo contracts.
  - An undo for construction.
  - Autosaves that don't freeze the game for about 0.7 s.
  - Loading only the image sizes the screen actually needs, and updating the minimap incrementally.
  - Fixes for phones: a bottom-sheet inspector, keeping gestures on the map, and a confirm step for touch placement.

When the plan arrives I'll pick the high-impact, low-risk batch and start implementing it. Items that touch the same code will be merged carefully (`app.js` is the file most of them share), and I'll check them with the node test suite and in the browser.

- Every item runs its named browser checks on a fresh no-store port.
- Items that change behaviour update README.md and ARCHITECTURE.md in their own sections.

3	Problem: routeHealth measures industries from their anchor tile (gameplay-insights.js:5 nearby(); used at :38-39). The simulation (stationCoverage, freightPair) and the Stop-hover ring measure to the nearest footprint tile (industryDistance, industry-sites.js:13). Result: 28.9% of legal stop tiles around 2x2/3x3 sites get a false 'No producer' or 'No buyer', and the card turns route-offline (app.js:494) while the route delivers.
4	
5	1. gameplay-insights.js
6	- Add `import { industryDistance } from './industry-sites.js'` and `const covers=(site,stop)=>industryDistance(site,stop)<=STATION_RADIUS`.
7	- In routeHealth: `sources = industries.filter(s=>covers(s,stops[0])&&INDUSTRIES[s.kind].outputs[cargo])` and `buyers = industries.filter(s=>covers(s,stops[1])&&INDUSTRIES[s.kind].inputs[cargo]&&!sources.includes(s))`. The source is excluded from buyers, as freightPair does.
8	- Keep nearby() (centre distance) for cities in townService, the passenger branch and townBuyer. This matches model.js:88.
9	- Do NOT switch to stationCoverage: the unit fixtures have no zones or spatial index.

# insights-footprint-fix — Fix false 'No producer' / 'No buyer' labels on working freight routes
files: ['fun/transport/gameplay-insights.js', 'fun/transport/model.js', 'fun/transport/tests/gameplay-insights.test.mjs']
Problem: routeHealth measures industries from their anchor tile (gameplay-insights.js:5 nearby(); used at :38-39). The simulation (stationCoverage, freightPair) and the Stop-hover ring measure to the nearest footprint tile (industryDistance, industry-sites.js:13). Result: 28.9% of legal stop tiles around 2x2/3x3 sites get a false 'No producer' or 'No buyer', and the card turns route-offline (app.js:494) while the route delivers.

1. gameplay-insights.js
- Add `import { industryDistance } from './industry-sites.js'` and `const covers=(site,stop)=>industryDistance(site,stop)<=STATION_RADIUS`.
- In routeHealth: `sources = industries.filter(s=>covers(s,stops[0])&&INDUSTRIES[s.kind].outputs[cargo])` and `buyers = industries.filter(s=>covers(s,stops[1])&&INDUSTRIES[s.kind].inputs[cargo]&&!sources.includes(s))`. The source is excluded from buyers, as freightPair does.
- Keep nearby() (centre distance) for cities in townService, the passenger branch and townBuyer. This matches model.js:88.
- Do NOT switch to stationCoverage: the unit fixtures have no zones or spatial index.
- Copy: the no-producer detail becomes `Add a producer of ${CARGO[cargo].name.toLowerCase()} within 5 tiles of the start.` (fixes 'a iron ore').

2. model.js addRoute failure message (about line 480): `Stations need a producer of ${cargo} and a matching factory or town within 5 tiles.` Only the message changes; the logic stays.

No save, simulation or determinism impact.
TESTS: gameplay-insights.test.mjs:
- Logging camp {footprint:2} at (10,12), sawmill {footprint:2} at (30,12), stop a at (16,13), stop b at (25,13), one loaded vehicle: routeHealth label is 'Running'.
- Move stop a to (17,13): 'No producer'.
- Real-model case: emptyGame; build iron-mine at 20,40 and steel-mill at 60,40; buildPath a road; add stops at 26,41 and 55,41; addRoute ok; advance 60 days. Expect state 'running' (today it is 'blocked'), and the no-producer detail does not match /\ba iron/.

Grep the tests for the old addRoute message and update any match. Run the full node suite.

# autosave-smooth-honest — Autosave without freezing vehicles, and never fail silently

Problem: persist() sets capturingSave, and frame() skips tick while it is set (app.js:871). Every vehicle stops for about 0.2 s at 512², 0.73 s at 1024² and 2.9 s at 2048², every 20 s and right after every successful build gesture (app.js:693). A failing periodic autosave is invisible: the #save-status text lives in the closed Game menu.

1. Debounce construction saves (app.js)
- `let constructionSaveTimer=0; function persistSoon(delay=3000){clearTimeout(constructionSaveTimer);constructionSaveTimer=setTimeout(()=>{constructionSaveTimer=0;persist();},delay);}`
- paintPath (line 693) uses persistSoon() instead of persist(). Explicit saves, route launches and the save dialog stay immediate.
- cancelPendingSave (line 550) also clears the timer. flushSave already writes synchronously on pagehide.

2. Keep vehicles moving inside the current day during capture
- frame line 871: `if(speed>0){if(!capturingSave)tick(game,elapsed*speed);else{const room=Math.floor(game.day+1e-8)+1-game.day-1e-6;if(room>0)tick(game,Math.min(elapsed*speed,room));}}`
- background-jobs.js captureGame: isCurrent also requires `Math.floor(game.day+1e-8)===startWholeDay` alongside the revision and networkRevision checks.
- world-transfer.js captureWorld snapshots routes synchronously next to `state=structuredClone(rest)`: `routeStates=routes.map(({path,...s})=>structuredClone(s))` and `paths=routes.map(r=>r.path)`. packRoutes uses these instead of reading the live route. Before returning, verify that routes.length and every path identity are unchanged; otherwise throw SnapshotChangedError.
- Periodic save (line 889): when speed>0, also require `game.day-Math.floor(game.day)<.25`, so the capture starts early in a day. Paused behaviour is unchanged.

3. Faster captureWorld tile loop
- Use a null-prototype TERRAIN_IDS lookup instead of indexOf.
- Add a fast path for tiles whose enumerable keys are exactly the core set (plus detail/publicRoad), with boolean road/rail/bridge/tunnel and null building/zone.
- Add a comment explaining the root cause: tiles fall into dictionary mode after `delete` (releaseTerrainObjects, bulldoze).
- Accept the change ONLY if an in-browser A/B wins in both states: freshly materialised tiles AND after 30+ simulated days or one grove bulldoze. The review measured a regression in the fresh state (29→45 ms) but 116→47 ms and 453→194 ms in real play.

4. Failure visibility
- `let saveHealthy=true`.
- saveFailed() sets #save-status to 'Save unavailable' and adds a .save-failed class. On the first transition only, it toasts (error) 'Autosave failed: browser storage is full or blocked. Delete older saves in Save / load (Ctrl+S) to free space.' It then sets data-alert and the aria-label 'Game menu · autosave failed' on #game-menu-button.
- Call it from persist()'s non-abort catch (regardless of notify; keep the explicit-save toast only when notify is set and the health toast did not just fire) and from flushSave's failure branch.
- After a failure, back off: `saveAt=performance.now()+40000`.
- saveFinished clears the alert and, after a failure, toasts 'Autosave is working again.'
- CSS: append to compact-play.css, right after the existing #game-menu-button rules: `#game-menu-button[data-alert]` shows an 8 px orange dot via ::after; `.save-failed` uses warning text colour.

All changes are in app.js pointer/key handlers and renderer picking.

1. Right-click during a left drag
- In Chrome a right press during a left drag arrives as pointermove(buttons&2), not pointerdown, so app.js:739 never runs and the release builds the stroke ($7,000 spent).
- In pointermove, inside `if(pointer&&pointer.id===e.pointerId)` and before the pan/preview logic: `if(!pointer.cancelled&&e.pointerType==='mouse'&&pointer.button===0&&!pointer.pan&&(e.buttons&2)){pointer.cancelled=true;preview=[];canvas.classList.remove('dragging');}` then `if(pointer.cancelled){pointer.lastX=e.clientX;pointer.lastY=e.clientY;$('#placement-tip').hidden=true;return;}`.
- Returning before updatePlacementTip means that function stays untouched.
- pointerup: immediately after `pointer=null…releasePointerCapture` add `if(p.cancelled){preview=[];$('#placement-tip').hidden=true;return;}`. It must come before the `p.button!==0` branch so both release orders work. The tool stays active; a plain right-click with no drag still leaves the tool.
- The contextmenu listener also cancels an active unpanned construction pointer.

2. Escape
- In keydown, `if(key==='escape'){ if(pointer&&!pointer.pan&&tool!=='inspect'){cancelGesture();return;} setTool('inspect');closeMobile();return;}`. A second Escape leaves the tool.

3. Edge clamp
- renderer.screenToTile and screenToVertex gain `{clamp=false}`. When pickGround returns null and clamp is set, unproject at ground level and clamp to [0,width-1]×[0,height-1] (vertices: round, same bounds).
- pickMapTile passes clamp only from pointermove while `pointer&&!pointer.pan&&!pointer.cancelled&&lineTools.has(pointer.tool)`. The preview and tip then end at the map edge instead of snapping to a line of about 125 tiles.
- The boundary guard at line 777 stays as a safety net.

4. Space after a mouse click
- Track `pointerFocus` with a capture pointerdown on document (the closest button/a/summary/[role=button]); clear it on focusin of any other element.
- Insert these listeners immediately before the `document.addEventListener('keydown'` line.
- Space branch (line 831): `const control=e.target.closest('button,a,summary,[role=button]'); if(control&&control!==pointerFocus)return;`. Otherwise run the existing code and set spaceConsumed.
- keyup: when Space was consumed, call preventDefault (stops Firefox's keyup activation).
- Keyboard-focused buttons keep native Space. Existing checks use locator.focus(), which fires no pointerdown, so they still pass.

In every case the toast is green (ok = count>0||skipped>0), and the tip stays stale after release. One side-slope tile paints the whole stroke red with a generic message; the median rejected stroke has only 3 offending tiles. The stop tip says 'Road stop · $3,200' even on grass. Policy decision: road/rail strokes become all-or-nothing, because a gapped road is useless. Zones and bulldoze stay partial, but say so honestly. model.buildPath keeps its documented partial policy for API callers.

1. model.js
- `export function buildProblem(game,tool,x,y,{money=game.money}={})` returns null (buildable, or 'Already built') or `{message,reason:'blocked'|'funds'|'terrain'}`.
- Extract every pre-mutation `return result(false,…)` of build() into it, in the same order with byte-identical messages: city/buildings/industries check funds before site problems; network tools, stops, ports, bulldoze and zones check funds last; raise/lower checks terraformProblem, then funds.
- build() starts with `const problem=buildProblem(game,tool,x,y); if(problem)return result(false,problem.message);`. 'level' keeps delegating.
- Also export `networkAlreadyBuilt(tile,tool)` (the `t[mode]&&(!bridge||t.bridge)&&(!tunnel||t.tunnel)` test).

2. terrain-engineering.js
- Internal networkTerrainIssue(game,x,y,mode,opts) returns null or {x,y,kind:'uneven'|'sideways'|'ramp-junction',at?}. For ramp-junction, `at` is the existing ramp neighbour that would gain a side link.

- New `networkTerrainPlanIssues(game,placements,limit=64)` collects issues de-duplicated by tile. networkTerrainPlanProblem = PlanIssues(…,1)[0] mapped to the old string.

- Walk placements with `let balance=game.money`. Each placement gets `state`: 'built' (unchanged, cost 0), 'blocked' (buildProblem with money:Infinity; store p.problem), 'slope' (in terrain issues), 'funds' (cost>balance), or 'ok' (balance-=cost).
