# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

description: "User's design direction for fun/transport — simple core loop, player never forced, TTD-like features only if they fit, long-horizon round-number achievements"

Direction the user gave for the Transport game on 2026-09-28, while features were being added:

- "Ensure the basic gameplay is simple and player is not forced to do anything." Every system must be optional and safe to ignore. That means no penalties for inaction, no hurtful deadlines, no nags or blocking modals, and goals framed as invitations. New complexity lives in on-demand UI, not on the default screen.
- "Anything to make it more similar to Transport Tycoon is welcome! but only fitting into our game design." That means TTD/OpenTTD feel and decisions adapted to the calm, elegant, two-stop-route design. No pastiche UI and no real brand names.
- "System of challenging achievements would be nice — based on round numbers and game progress after e.g. 100 years of playing."

- "The reward for cargo should be distance/time (the faster and further, the more money)" — TTD-style: pay grows with distance and falls with transit time.
- "Can you also add airports" — a fourth mode (air), art must be code-drawn here (no image generator available).
- "Double down on city building side — extending tycoon games, player will also be able to invest in cities, build housing, industry, commerce zones, to bring more business/demand to the area" — the city side should be a second pillar that feeds transport demand, with visible returns on investment.

**Why:** the user wants depth for long play without making the casual loop harder or pressuring players.
**How to apply:** when proposing or reviewing transport features, check them against these rules first. Prefer recognition (titles, achievements, headlines) over pressure (closures, penalties). See [[transport-playability-overhaul]].

Direction the user gave for the Transport game on 2026-09-28, while features were being added:
- "Can you also add airports" — a fourth mode (air), art must be code-drawn here (no image generator available).

- "Double down on city building side — extending tycoon games, player will also be able to invest in cities, build housing, industry, commerce zones, to bring more business/demand to the area" — the city side should be a second pillar that feeds transport demand, with visible returns on investment.
+- "Put some good effort into UI — colors, fonts, icons, labels, interconnection, fluency, minimalism." → a UI design system (fun/transport/DESIGN.md) applied last across every surface.
**Why:** the user wants depth for long play without making the casual loop harder or pressuring players.

**How to apply:** when proposing or reviewing transport features, check them against these rules first. Prefer recognition (titles, achievements, headlines) over pressure (closures, penalties). See [[transport-playability-overhaul]].

content.text:
I've started a dedicated UI design pass, and it will shape all the new screens too.

1. **Audit:** an agent screenshots every UI state on desktop and phone. It lists every colour, font size, icon source, label pattern and entity mention, and notes whether each mention links to the map. It then ranks the problems.
2. **Three competing directions:** each stays within the Protocodus look (Space Grotesk, dark green, orange, light panels) and takes a different angle:
   - **Wayfinding:** station signage and route-map line colours, strict pictograms.
   - **Atlas:** the UI as the map's legend and margin, so the painted map stands out.
   - **Quiet instrument:** minimal controls, numbers first, details revealed only when needed.

   Each designer builds a rendered mockup over a real game screenshot, looks at it and iterates.
3. **Judging:** three judges score the directions from the player's view, a visual-design view and an engineering view. They pick a winner and borrow the best ideas from the others.
4. **Final system:** the result is written up as `fun/transport/DESIGN.md`, split into implementation items. Those cover colour and type tokens, one icon language, labels and messages, clickable town/industry/stop/route/vehicle/cargo references that highlight on the map, smooth transitions, a minimal default screen, and mobile polish.

Every later implementer gets `DESIGN.md`, so the airports, city-investment and Transport Tycoon screens are built in the new style. The UI batches run last and sweep every screen, including the new ones.

**Current queue:**
1. The plan batches, which are running now.
2. Transport Tycoon mechanics and achievements.
3. Airports and distance × speed pay.
4. City investment.
5. UI system.
6. Simplicity fixes.
7. Final review, full verification, then the push to `main`.

I'll assemble the batches as each design run finishes.

- unloadVehicle has a clean `if(delivered>0)` hook point.
- `history.month` is the calendarMonth index. The inflation index is constant within a year, so the 1950-dollar conversion is exact.
- Route and top-level fields pass through route-save-codec and world-transfer unchanged.
- Money is bounded at 1e12 in validateGame, so billion-nominal fits.

- A fully zoned, served town reaches 5,476 in year 1 and then stays flat. 5,000 is a fair silver.
- A 100-tile passenger rail line earns about $1.31M a year in 1950 dollars. In the sim that is the sum of duplicate routes on one line, which fleet-per-route consolidates onto one route.
- All chain products have consumers (taiga 12, tundra 10, desert 11).
- A vehicle carries 1,000 units only from 1981 (ships) or 2001 (trains).

2. The Shipping family. "Buy N ships" is purchasing, not mastery, and Fleet already covers it.

9. Cargo targets are now static flags.

11. The yearly profit reads company-report-credit's `game.annual` entry.

content.text:
The Transport Tycoon design pass finished, and all 9 mechanics were accepted after the critics revised them:

- **Achievements:** 38 records in bronze, silver, gold and platinum, from 100,000 deliveries up to a debt-free century, plus hidden ones.
  - Money is measured in 1950 dollars, so inflation doesn't make them trivial late on.
  - They're pure recognition: an on-demand dialog and one calm notice when you earn one.
  - The critic removed a streak that resets and a "buy N ships" achievement, because those would pressure the player.
- **Company rating and titles:** a 0–1000 score, Engineer up to Tycoon, and an end-of-century review in 2050.
- **Named vehicle models and vehicle age:** fictional model names per mode, a gentle "Old" nudge, and profit this year and last year on each route card.
- **Headlines:** "Citizens celebrate — first bus arrives in Cedarbridge" and other rare big moments.
- **Full load:** a per-route toggle, off by default.
- **Industries opening:** new industries appear over time. Closures were dropped because they would pressure the player.
- **Town opinion with town actions:** this will likely be merged into the city-investment design that's still running.
- **Mail between towns.**
- **Transit-time payment:** this will be replaced by your distance × speed version, which is still being designed.

The simplicity audit found 19 issues, including 5 serious ones:
- Routes flagged "busy" push the player to act, so that state becomes plain "Running".
- A factory whose storage is full stops paying for deliveries. It will now always pay.
- Unmet town needs stop growth entirely. They will now only slow it.
- A folded goal card reopens every time the goal changes. It will now stay folded.
- The milestone ladder counts things in a fixed order; it will count them whenever you do them.

I've written those fixes into the specs of the 14 planned items that haven't started yet, so they get built right the first time. The rest go into a final "never forced" batch. That batch also adds a test that runs a company for 30 years with no player input and checks it never loses money or gets nagged.

**Still running:**
- **Implementation:** batch 2 is fully integrated. Batch 3 (fleets per route, terrain-following drags, route highlighting, older browser checks fixed) is underway.
- **Design:** airports with distance × speed pay, city investment, and the UI system are still in progress.

<result>{"vision":"Towns become a second business that feeds transport. Each town is a small market with three sides the player can grow, and each side makes business for the transport company.
- Homes: the people who travel (passengers, and mail once ttd-mail lands) and who shop.
- Shops: each month they want a measured amount of food, household goods (furniture in taiga, goods in tundra and desert), fuel and, while the town is building, stone and cement.
- Workshops: the town's light industry. Industrial zones and a new placeable 2×2 Workshop take in delivered materials (lumber, steel, glass, wire) and send out furniture, machinery or goods that must travel to another town.

The inspector's collapsed 'Town economy' section shows this as three demand bars (Homes, Shops, Workshops), a 'Shops want each month' list, the town's workshops and, where the company owns land, its property and returns.

**Player verbs.** All four are optional and none is on the default screen.
1. Paint zones. They stay cheap: you buy the plot, developers build on it, and you collect ground rent.
2. Place buildings from the catalog, including the new Workshop. They cost more and appear at once, and you collect full rent. A Workshop can be expanded to level 3. Buildings you own can be sold back to the town for 60% of their value.
3. Fund development at the town hall. This absorbs ttd-town-authority's 'Fund new buildings': the town builds its own homes about twice as fast, and your zones there develop twice as fast even without service.
4. Watch the returns: rent floats above your towns at month end, each town keeps a 12-month ledger, and the company report gains a Property section.

**Loops with transport.**
- Regular passenger service raises Homes demand, and passengers you bring become shoppers who raise Shops demand.
- Freight that fills a town's wants earns a 25% market bonus on the wanted amount and keeps its shops' rent high.
- Materials you deliver to workshops come out as finished goods, which make a second, outbound freight route.
- More homes raise shop wants and passenger and mail supply. More shops widen what a town wants. More workshops create more buyers and more producers.
- Demand bars only ever speed up the matching zones, never slow them.

**Optional and simple.**
- Towns keep accepting every delivery at the full fare. The market bonus is only extra money on top.
- Property has no upkeep and never loses value. Occupancy has floors of 60% for homes, 40% for shops and 30% for workshops.
- No notices, deadlines, taxes or closures. Nothing new appears on the HUD or map by default. The only map addition is a monthly rent pill, which follows the existing Income layer.
- Sims confirm the starter company left alone for 30 years has the same cash curve, zero warnings and the same nextId.

**How it pays back** (calibrated in node sims, 1950 dollars):
- A residential 2×2 plot block ($1,680) earns about $59 a month and pays back in about 3 years, including roughly a year of development.
- A fully zoned town (74 plots, $32k) grows from 1,220 to 3,630 residents and earns about $900 a month in ground rent.
- Catalog homes pay back in about 5.75 years. A grocer pays back in about 5 years when stocked and 12 years or more when not.
- Shops you also stock pay back in about a year: 3 grocers raise wants by 29 food a month, worth +$1.3k a month in market bonus plus $239 rent.
- Two workshop blocks ($7k) sustain about 90 lumber a month in and 45 furniture a month out, worth about $21k a month in fares for three trucks.
- Transport stays the main engine: a fully developed town's rent is about a quarter of one bus. The city pillar's value is the new freight it creates and the long-horizon, land-bounded property it builds.","evidence":"Nothing in the repository was edited. - 12 zones painted beside Alderbrook developed to levels 1–2 within 150 days at 8×.
- Population rose only 884 → 894: the zones took the same road-side plots organic growth fills. Alderbrook is ringed by rock (56 grass tiles against 305 rock or mountain within 10), so the sims use a flat two-town fixture instead.

FINDING 1: passenger supply is abundant (e3.mjs)
The fixture towns (about 1,200 residents, 40 tiles apart) give fares per month in years 2–3:

| Buses | Fares / month | Waiting in A |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $4.0k | 1,098 |
| 4 | $16.1k | 1,074 |
| 8 | $32.2k | 1,027 |
| 12 | $48.3k | 967 |

- Adding 20 residential zones (+686 residents) changed fares by ±2%.
- Each town generates about 0.35 trips per resident a month (675 trips for 1,906 residents), while a bus carries about 23 per end a month.
- So housing only lifts fares at rail or airport scale. The city pillar's transport value has to come from freight: wants plus the market bonus, and workshops.

FINDING 2: food wants and the market bonus (e4.mjs; a refilled food plant 19 tiles from a 1,220-resident town)

| Food trucks | Base fares / month | Bonus / month |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $11.1k | $2.2k |
| 2 | $22.0k | $4.1k |
| 4 | $40.0k | $4.2k (capped by wants 90) |

- 2 blocks ($7,040) reached 6 levels by day about 151. They processed 90 lumber a month at 100% utilization into 45 furniture.

- 4 blocks: $24.9k + $17.4k/month with 4 + 2 trucks.

content.text:
The city-investment design is done. All 5 parts were accepted after the critics revised them:

1. **Town economy:** each town's inspector gets a collapsed section with demand bars for homes, shops and workshops, plus a list of what its shops want each month (food, household goods, fuel, building materials). Deliveries that fill those wants earn a 25% bonus. Towns still accept everything at full fare, so ignoring the section costs nothing.
2. **Workshops:** industrial zones and a new placeable 2×2 Workshop take in lumber, steel, glass or wire and turn out furniture, machinery or goods for other towns. This is the biggest source of new freight. In the simulation, two workshop blocks costing $7k supported about $21k a month in fares.
3. **Company property:** zones you paint earn ground rent, and buildings you place earn full rent. Rent rises with service but never falls below a floor, and there's no upkeep. Rent appears above towns at month end, and you can sell back at 60% of value. A home block pays back in about 3 years, and a stocked shop in about a year.
4. **Town hall:** a single "Fund development" action makes the town build faster and speeds up your own zones there. It replaces the separate "fund new buildings" action from the Transport Tycoon design.
5. **Investment forecast and returns:** the Build → Town placement tip shows what an investment will bring, each town keeps a 12-month ledger, your property is outlined, and the Towns list tags towns where you own property.

The critics fixed two money exploits in the property design and a workshop placement bug. They also checked that a company left alone for 30 years earns exactly what it did before.

**Current state:**
- **Implementation:** batch 3 is 3 of 5 done (fleets per route, terrain-following drags, service-gated growth). Route highlighting and the fixes to the older browser checks are still running.
- **Still designing:** airports (the first attempt stalled and was restarted), distance × speed pay, and the UI audit.

This adds air as a fourth transport mode in the game's own gentle style, without TTD pastiche or real brands.

- Air travel arrives on 1 January 1952. Before that, Build → Network shows a greyed Airport card with the date. The first minutes stay simple, and the date becomes a quiet TTD-style moment. Companies already past 1952 can build airports straight away.
- An airport is a 6 × 2 site: runway, apron, a 1950s terminal with a glass hall and spectator terrace, a control tower, a hangar, a fuel depot and a windsock. It costs $60,000, versus $12,000 for a train station. It needs clear, dry, level land and serves towns within 7 tiles.
- An air route joins two airports at least 16 tiles apart and needs no network. Planes fly a straight line. On every visit they land, roll out, taxi to a stand, board, taxi out and take off the other way. Everything is drawn natively, with altitude, soft shadows and night lights.
- Planes are fast (12 tiles a day), carry a moderate 40 seats (56 on the 1952 debut), and are expensive to buy ($150k base) and run. They carry passengers, and mail once ttd-mail lands, never freight.
- The economics make planes a mid- to late-game choice that shines on long routes:
  - trains keep short hops;
  - at 50 tiles, air roughly matches rail without any track;
  - at 100 tiles and more, air wins, clearly so under ttd-cargo-payment.
- Nothing is forced. There are no crashes, collisions, noise complaints, breakdowns or chores. A company that never builds an airport is byte-identical to today.

Implementation stays small because of one representation choice. A flight is saved as a 4-connected staircase along the straight line between the two airport anchors. Every existing path invariant therefore holds unchanged: the save codec, validation, fares by path length, and progress-based spacing. Only air's movement speed and drawn position are special-cased.","evidence":"All paths are under `REDACTED`. The scratch dir is lost on reboot.

## In-game composites
Made with `proto-game2.mjs`: the live game (seed 1847, Cedar Falls) renders a real site, and the prototype art is composited with the renderer's own projection, depth-sorted. The planes are placed by `air-flight.js` at real choreography states. All three zooms at DPR 1 and 2, day and night, are in `shots/proto2/airport-z{0.5,1,2}-dpr{1,2}-{day,night}.png`.

- **Town zoom.** Two airports (x and y axes) read as a coherent airfield among the painted houses.
  - The tower is a landmark about the height of a 3-storey civic building.
  - Parked, taxiing, rolling-out and take-off planes are visible, with the masts, depot and hangar.
- **Detail zoom** (`crop-z2.png`, `airport-z2-dpr2-day.png`):
  - glazed terminal hall, orange canopy, terrace railing, tower balcony and cab, ribbed hangar and depot tanks;
  - the buildings are a little cleaner-illustrative than the raster houses but sit in the same world;

content.text:
The airport and distance × speed pay designs are done and accepted.

**Airports** (the prototype art looks right in-game, see below):
- **Timing and site:** air travel arrives on 1 January 1952 as a quiet dated moment. Before that, the Airport card is greyed out. An airport is a 6×2 site with a runway, apron, terminal, control tower, hangar, fuel depot and windsock. It costs $60k (a train station is $12k) and serves towns within 7 tiles.
- **Flights:** planes fly straight between two airports at least 16 tiles apart, with no network needed. They land, taxi, board and take off again. They carry passengers (and mail later), 40–56 seats, and are fast but expensive.
- **Economics:** rail stays better on short hops, air matches rail at about 50 tiles and wins from 100 tiles, clearly so under the new pay rule.
- **Art:** it's drawn in code and I checked the prototype composited into a real game scene. At Town zoom the towers, terminals, hangars and parked planes sit naturally among the painted houses. At night the runway edge lights, beacons and aircraft navigation lights match the game's night look. Desert and tundra variants exist, with snow on the roofs.
- **Critic:** it fixed two real bugs: clicking a runway tile showed "Open countryside", and the first-route checklist wrongly counted airports as stops.

**Pay by distance and speed:** delivery pay now grows with distance and falls with transit time, so faster vehicles and longer hauls earn more. Every fare in the game goes through one place, which keeps the change contained. The details show only on demand: a payment-rates chart, a line on each route card, and the forecast.

**Still running:**
- **UI system design:** the audit is still in progress.
- **Implementation:** batch 3 is finishing (route highlighting and the fixes to the older browser checks).

When the UI design is done, I'll assemble everything designed so far into the next round of batches: Transport Tycoon, airports, pay, city investment, UI and the simplicity pass.

JUDGE winner wayfinding | [('wayfinding', 72), ('atlas', 66), ('quiet-instrument', 73)]
  graft: Base on wayfinding. Its line bullets, roundels, nameplates and saturated casing palette are the only map layer that lets the player read the network at a glance. The audit shows that today's pastels vanish on moss and water. Graft these ideas from the other two directions.

FROM QUIET-INSTRUMENT
(1) Lighter always-on chrome. Keep the goal as a collapsed line by default and show the ladder only on demand. Consider board-coloured (light) HUD plates, or a slimmer enamel plate, if playtests find fou
JUDGE winner quiet-instrument | [('wayfinding', 67), ('atlas', 65), ('quiet-instrument', 74)]
  graft: Keep quiet-instrument's frame as it is: light paper rails, dark only for transient surfaces, one orange \"waiting on you\" signal, hairline rows instead of cards, the linked hover state across all matching data-ref elements, and a drawer that grows from the rail. Graft these onto it.

FROM WAYFINDING
1. Bullet shape by mode:
   - road: rounded square
   - rail: circle
   - water: pill
   - air (future airports): diamond
   The number and colour stay; the shape carries the mode without letters. A
JUDGE winner quiet-instrument | [('wayfinding', 69), ('atlas', 66), ('quiet-instrument', 74)]
  graft: Winner: quiet instrument. It has the lowest regression risk and the least art or save migration, it keeps the map most clearly the hero, and its interconnection has the cheapest path through the existing highlightRoute and change-keyed render loop. Graft these ideas onto it.

1. Raise the type floor to 12 px, with 14 px body on phones. This closes instrument's main accessibility gap.
2. Fix the line palette:

# Transport UI system

This file defines the UI system for `fun/transport`, and every UI change follows it. If code disagrees with this file, the code is wrong, unless this file changes in the same commit with the reason. Token values are defined here and copied into `tokens.css` (CSS custom properties) and `design-tokens.js` (canvas and JS). `tests/design-tokens.test.mjs` checks that all three match.

Some feature specs set their own colours, sizes or wording, such as literal hex values, a kicker joined with a middle dot, or "Next goal" eyebrows. Where they disagree with this file, this file wins, and the UI items restyle those parts.

---

## 1. What the UI is for

Transport is a calm isometric game about transport and town building. The map is generated and painterly (moss greens, turquoise water, warm roofs), and it is the hero. The UI is the instrument panel around its edges.

The UI has one job. It lets the player read the state of the world and act on it in as few obvious steps as possible. The player moves between the map and the panels without losing their place.

The players know Transport Tycoon, OpenTTD, Mini Motorways and Cities, and they want an elegant browser game, not a spreadsheet. The basic loop stays simple, and the player never has to open anything.

Transport Tycoon touches appear only where they fit: numbered routes, a newspaper for big moments, company records. Towns are the second pillar and get the same visual rigour as routes.

The brand is Protocodus: Space Grotesk, dark green ink, one orange accent (the orange t tile) and warm light paper.

## 2. Principles

1. **The map is the hero.** The default screen is the map, three small rails (navigation, instruments, zoom) and a one-line goal. Everything else opens when asked for and closes without leaving anything behind.
2. **A surface shows how long it lives.**
   - Paper rails are always there (elevation e1).
   - Paper sheets open when the player asks: the drawer, the inspector, the goal ladder, menus and popovers (e2).
   - Ink surfaces either go away on their own or follow the pointer: toasts, tooltips, placement tips, the selection tag, edge pointers and the back chip (e3).
   - Dialogs are paper over a scrim and stop map interaction (e4).
   - World labels drawn on the map are paper plates: town nameplates, delivery and rent floaters, industry badges. They belong to the world, not to the instrument.
3. **One signal.** Orange means "here, now, waiting on you". It marks:
   - the selection;
   - keyboard focus;
   - the current goal step;
   - the paused clock;
   - unread News.

   The t tile is the only orange that is always on screen. At most one orange-filled call to action is visible at a time: the action of the current goal step. The lit pause segment is a state, not a call to action.
4. **One memorable element: the line.** A route is shown as a numbered bullet in its line colour, shaped by its mode, together with a strip diagram of its state. This line language is used on the map and in rows, toasts, goals, forms and contracts. Everything else stays quiet.
5. **Everything named is a reference.** Every mention of a town, industry, stop, route, vehicle or cargo uses the same clickable, hoverable reference, and that reference finds the thing on the map.
6. **Motion only answers.** Things move when the player acts, or to show a change the player caused. Nothing loops except the loading screen.
7. **Plain words, one name per thing.** An action keeps its name from the button to the result. Errors say what happened and how to fix it.
8. **Structure means something.** A border, divider, number, colour or weight must carry information. If it does not, remove it.

## 3. Decisions (how the three proposals were merged)

Three directions were mocked up on real frames of the game and judged:

- **Wayfinding:** dark enamel HUD, transit bullets.
- **Atlas:** paper collar, the UI as the map's margin.
- **Quiet instrument:** light rails, dark means transient.

Two of three judges chose quiet instrument as the base, and all three wanted parts of wayfinding's network language. This system is quiet instrument's frame with wayfinding's line and map language, plus atlas's error handling, selection mark and context aids. Do not reopen these decisions without new evidence from the live game.

| Topic | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome | Light paper rails. Ink only for transient surfaces. | Dark enamel slabs over the art pulled the eye away from the map (two judges). Light rails match the brand and today's DOM, and need the least CSS churn. |
| Route identity | Number + line colour + bullet shape by mode: road square, rail circle, water pill, air diamond. | Colour alone fails beyond 6 routes and for colour-blind players. Shape shows the mode without letters. Airports need no new chrome. |
| Line palette | 9 colours that alternate deep (white numerals) and light (ink numerals). No green, teal or orange. | Once land, water and signal hues are excluded, pastels alone run out of distinct hues. Per-line numeral colour is real transit practice. Checked on the live map: deep lines with a paper halo and light lines with an ink casing both read on moss, roads and river. Today's pastel teal vanished on the river. |
| Map labels | Keep the paper nameplate pills. Replace the lettered B/T stop sign with a roundel that carries route bullets. | Atlas's stroke-halo labels looked crude over roofs. The B sign collided with town names. |
| Selection | Orange footprint outline on a paper casing, plus an ink name tag. | Quiet instrument's pale outline was too faint. Orange means here. |
| Panel ↔ map | Linked state on every matching reference, a map highlight, and an edge pointer for off-screen targets. | Atlas's leader lines were restless and looked like rendering glitches. |
| Type | Space Grotesk only. 14 px body. 12 px floor everywhere, canvas included. | Quiet instrument's 11 px floor was marginal on phones. |

print(len(s)); print([ (b['name'], [i['id'] for i in b['items']]) for b in batches])
EOF

export const meta = {
  name: 'transport-phase2',
  description: 'Phase 2 of the Transport overhaul: UI system, Transport Tycoon mechanics, airports, cargo pay, city investment, simplicity guardrails; then final review, fix and verify',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Implement', detail: 'one agent per item, each in its own git worktree' },
    { title: 'Merge', detail: 'squash-merge the batch, run suites and a smoke play' },
    { title: 'Final review', detail: 'code review, play-tests, design system, simplicity, perf, long play' },
    { title: 'Fix', detail: 'verify and fix confirmed review findings' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'full node suite, full browser-check sweep, legacy saves' },
  ],
}

const SP = 'REDACTED'
const PLANS = '/Users/vojta/.claude/plans/transport-overhaul'
const SPECS = `${PLANS}/specs`
const REPO = '/Users/vojta/Dev/protocodus.github.io'
const BRANCH = 'transport-playability'
const PW = '/Users/vojta/Dev/evangelist-exchange/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'
const DIFF_BASE = args.diffBase
const landed = [...args.landed]

const GAME = `The browser game "Transport" lives in fun/transport of the repo ${REPO} — an isometric transport & city-building tycoon game (static ES modules, no build step, Canvas 2D; app.js UI/input, model.js simulation, renderer.js, many modules; README.md is the player guide, ARCHITECTURE.md the module reference, PERFORMANCE.md perf notes). It is being overhauled on branch ${BRANCH}; each item lands as one squash commit. Per-item specs live in ${SPECS}/<id>.md (authoritative; read yours fully, including any appended guardrail and ordering notes), shared merge/safety rules in ${SPECS}/_rules.md.
THE USER'S DESIGN PRINCIPLES (hard requirements): the basic gameplay stays simple and the player is never forced to do anything (every system optional and safe to ignore, no penalties for inaction, new complexity behind on-demand UI); Transport Tycoon-like features only where they fit this calm, elegant game; long-horizon round-number achievements; cargo pay grows with distance and speed; the city side is a second pillar that creates transport demand; the UI gets real care — colours, fonts, icons, labels, interconnection, fluency, minimalism.
UI SYSTEM: every UI change follows the design system document. It is committed as fun/transport/DESIGN.md by the first UI item (ui-tokens-and-type); until that has landed read ${SPECS}/_DESIGN.md. If a spec's literal colours, sizes or wording disagree with DESIGN.md, DESIGN.md wins.
Browser tooling: Playwright at ${PW}; launch chromium with {channel:'chrome', headless:true, args:['--use-angle=metal','--enable-gpu','--ignore-gpu-blocklist']}. Chrome CANNOT launch inside the Bash sandbox, so every node command that starts a browser, every background server start, and kill/pkill/lsof must run with dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true. Browser checks read TRANSPORT_URL and TRANSPORT_PLAYWRIGHT (and often TRANSPORT_OUTPUT). The game opens at a start menu: fun/transport/tests/browser-start.mjs has createWorldFromMenu/loadAutosaveFromMenu/waitForGameReady/openGameAction; window.transport exposes {game, renderer, speed, setSpeed, setTool, setView, inspect, persist}. No-cache static server: python3 ${PLANS}/serve.py <port> <root-dir>. Scratch space: ${SP} (may vanish on reboot; keep nothing important only there).
Code style: match the surrounding code — dense one-line functions, same naming and idioms, sparse comments; never reformat or reflow existing lines; no new dependencies. model.js stays DOM-free. Saves stay backward compatible (new fields optional, validated, defaulted) and the simulation deterministic (randomAt; notify() consumes nextId, so avoid new notify() calls on simulation paths unless the spec allows it).`

const IMPL = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    id: { type: 'string' },
    status: { type: 'string', enum: ['done', 'partial', 'failed'] },
    branch: { type: 'string' },
    sha: { type: 'string', description: 'final commit sha on the branch (empty if nothing committed)' },
    summary: { type: 'string' },
    deviations: { type: 'string' },
    nodeTests: { type: 'string' },
    browserChecks: { type: 'string' },
    visualCheck: { type: 'string' },
    notesForMerger: { type: 'string' },
  },
  required: ['id', 'status', 'branch', 'sha', 'summary', 'deviations', 'nodeTests', 'browserChecks', 'visualCheck', 'notesForMerger'],
}
const MERGE = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    sha: { type: 'string' },
    merged: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    skipped: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'string' }, reason: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['id', 'reason'] } },
    conflictNotes: { type: 'string' },
    nodeTests: { type: 'string' },
    browserChecks: { type: 'string' },
    smoke: { type: 'string' },
    integrationFixes: { type: 'string' },
    openIssues: { type: 'string' },
  },
  required: ['sha', 'merged', 'skipped', 'conflictNotes', 'nodeTests', 'browserChecks', 'smoke', 'integrationFixes', 'openIssues'],
}

const smokeStep = (tag) => `Smoke play with a Playwright script in ${SP}/merge/${tag}/: fresh taiga world (seed 1847) via the start menu at 1440x900; open the drawers and dialogs; build a short road and stops; create a route through the form; exercise every feature merged in this batch; run 8x for 30 s; then the essentials on a 390x844 touch viewport. Collect console and page errors; take screenshots and LOOK at them with Read — judge whether the result follows DESIGN.md, reads clearly and does not clutter. Anything broken by the combination of items is your job to fix.`

function implPrompt(it, batch, base, port) {
  const others = batch.items.filter(o => o.id !== it.id).map(o => `- ${o.id} — ${o.title}`).join('\n') || '- none'
  return `${GAME}

YOUR TASK: implement exactly ONE item: "${it.id}" — ${it.title}.
Read your full spec first: ${SPECS}/${it.id}.md (Spec section authoritative; appended guardrail and ordering notes override it). Read ${SPECS}/_rules.md and the UI system (DESIGN.md or ${SPECS}/_DESIGN.md). Then read the code you will touch — the code has moved on since specs were written, so re-locate functions by name, and build on what landed instead of duplicating it.
ALREADY LANDED on your base (specs for each in ${SPECS}/): ${landed.join(', ')}.

WORKTREE: you run in your own private git worktree (your cwd; root via git rev-parse --show-toplevel).
1. git rev-parse HEAD must equal ${base}; if not, git reset --hard ${base} (private worktree, safe).
2. git checkout -B tp/${it.id}
Edit only inside this worktree. Never modify ${REPO} (the main checkout) or other worktrees.

PARALLEL ITEMS in this batch (other worktrees, squash-merged with yours afterwards):
${others}
Stay inside your spec's scope; touch only the functions/lines your spec and its notes name in shared hot files; never reflow existing lines; new CSS goes on new lines in the stylesheet your spec (or DESIGN.md's one-stylesheet-per-surface rule) names.

SERVER AND BROWSER: python3 ${PLANS}/serve.py ${port} <your-worktree-root> in the background (run_in_background, dangerouslyDisableSandbox). URL http://127.0.0.1:${port}/fun/transport/. Browser checks: TRANSPORT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:${port}/fun/transport/ TRANSPORT_PLAYWRIGHT=${PW} TRANSPORT_OUTPUT=${SP}/impl/${it.id}/<check> node fun/transport/tests/<check>.mjs (dangerouslyDisableSandbox). Kill your server when done.

VERIFY: add the spec's node tests (first, and see them fail), implement until green; run the FULL node suite from your worktree root (node --test --test-concurrency=3 fun/transport/tests/*.test.mjs) — fully green, only deliberately changed expectations updated; run the browser checks your spec names, with its new assertions; for anything visible take screenshots in the real game and LOOK at them, judging against DESIGN.md and the user's principles, and iterate. Update README.md / ARCHITECTURE.md sections your spec names, in their existing voice.

COMMIT on tp/${it.id}: check git status (never commit screenshots, scratch or .playwright-mcp), git add the changed files under fun/transport, commit "<type>(transport): <concise summary>" (feat/fix/perf) with a short body and the final line
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Do not push or merge. If part of the spec is wrong or infeasible, adapt sensibly and report the deviation; if blocked, commit what is solid and report "partial".`
}

function mergePrompt(batch, tag, impls, base) {
  return `${GAME}

YOU ARE THE INTEGRATOR for ${batch.name}. Work in the main checkout ${REPO} on branch ${BRANCH} (absolute paths). Implementers worked in parallel private worktrees from base ${base} and committed to branches tp/<id>. Reports:
${JSON.stringify(impls, null, 1)}

1. git -C ${REPO} status must be clean on ${BRANCH} at HEAD ${base}; if not, investigate and report — never discard what you did not create.
2. Integrate in this order: ${batch.items.map(i => i.id).join(', ')}. For each with a commit: git merge --squash <sha>; resolve conflicts preserving BOTH sides' intent (read both specs in ${SPECS}/; hand-merge long lines carefully; never drop functionality); commit with the implementer's message (git log -1 --format=%B <sha>). One commit per item. Skip an unusable item and say why.
3. node --check every changed JS file; full node suite (node --test --test-concurrency=4 fun/transport/tests/*.test.mjs) must be green; run the union of the batch specs' browser checks against http://127.0.0.1:8841/fun/transport/ (start python3 ${PLANS}/serve.py 8841 ${REPO} in the background with dangerouslyDisableSandbox if curl gets no 200), at most 3 concurrently, env TRANSPORT_URL, TRANSPORT_PLAYWRIGHT=${PW}, TRANSPORT_OUTPUT=${SP}/merge/${tag}/<check>.
4. ${smokeStep(tag)}
5. Fix integration problems minimally in the house style; commit "fix(transport): integrate ${tag}" with a body and the final line Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>.
Never push; never touch main; never delete tp/* branches; only git reset --hard HEAD / git merge --abort to back out an in-progress item merge. Return sha = git rev-parse HEAD and merged = item ids.`
}

let base = args.base
const batchReports = []
for (let b = 0; b < args.batches.length; b++) {
  const batch = args.batches[b]
  log(`${batch.name}: implementing ${batch.items.length} item(s) from ${base.slice(0, 8)}`)
  const impls = await parallel(batch.items.map((it, i) => () =>
    agent(implPrompt(it, batch, base, 9250 + b * 10 + i), { label: `impl:${it.id}`, phase: 'Implement', isolation: 'worktree', schema: IMPL })))
  const reports = batch.items.map((it, i) => impls[i] || { id: it.id, status: 'failed', branch: `tp/${it.id}`, sha: '', summary: 'agent returned nothing', deviations: '', nodeTests: '', browserChecks: '', visualCheck: '', notesForMerger: '' })
  log(`${batch.name}: ${reports.filter(r => r.status !== 'failed' && r.sha).length}/${reports.length} items committed`)
  const tag = `p2-${b + 1}`
  const merged = await agent(mergePrompt(batch, tag, reports, base), { label: `merge:${tag}`, phase: 'Merge', schema: MERGE })
  if (!merged || !merged.sha) { log(`merge of ${batch.name} failed; stopping`); batchReports.push({ batch: batch.name, reports, merged }); return { head: base, batchReports, stopped: true } }
  base = merged.sha
  landed.push(...merged.merged)
  batchReports.push({ batch: batch.name, reports, merged })
  log(`${batch.name}: merged ${merged.merged.length}, skipped ${merged.skipped.length}; head ${base.slice(0, 8)}`)
}

phase('Final review')
const FINDINGS = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {

  },
  required: ['summary', 'findings'],
}
const REVIEWERS = [
  { key: 'correctness-simulation', prompt: `Adversarially review the simulation/save side of the full diff ${DIFF_BASE}..${base} (git -C ${REPO} diff ${DIFF_BASE} ${base} -- fun/transport; model.js, settlements.js, industry-simulation.js, environment.js, economy/pricing, contracts, milestones, achievements, company rating, mail, airports, town authority/market/workshops/property, construction-plan/undo, network-router, save codecs, gameplay-insights, route-planner). Look for determinism breaks, save round-trip and legacy-save failures, validateGame gaps, money exploits (undo refunds, sell/buy loops, property sell-back, credit, contracts, market bonus), broken invariants between items. const PLANS = '/Users/vojta/.claude/plans/transport-overhaul'
const SPECS = `${PLANS}/specs`
const REPO = '/Users/vojta/Dev/protocodus.github.io'
const BRANCH = 'transport-playability'

const DIFF_BASE = args.diffBase
const landed = [...args.landed]

const GAME = `The browser game "Transport" lives in fun/transport of the repo ${REPO} — an isometric transport & city-building tycoon game (static ES modules, no build step, Canvas 2D; app.js UI/input, model.js simulation, renderer.js, many modules; README.md is the player guide, ARCHITECTURE.md the module reference, PERFORMANCE.md perf notes). It is being overhauled on branch ${BRANCH}; each item lands as one squash commit. Per-item specs live in ${SPECS}/<id>.md (authoritative; read yours fully, including any appended guardrail and ordering notes), shared merge/safety rules in ${SPECS}/_rules.md.
THE USER'S DESIGN PRINCIPLES (hard requirements): the basic gameplay stays simple and the player is never forced to do anything (every system optional and safe to ignore, no penalties for inaction, new complexity behind on-demand UI); Transport Tycoon-like features only where they fit this calm, elegant game; long-horizon round-number achievements; cargo pay grows with distance and speed; the city side is a second pillar that creates transport demand; the UI gets real care — colours, fonts, icons, labels, interconnection, fluency, minimalism.
UI SYSTEM: every UI change follows the design system document. It is committed as fun/transport/DESIGN.md by the first UI item (ui-tokens-and-type); until that has landed read ${SPECS}/_DESIGN.md. If a spec's literal colours, sizes or wording disagree with DESIGN.md, DESIGN.md wins.
Browser tooling: Playwright at ${PW}; launch chromium with {channel:'chrome', headless:true, args:['--use-angle=metal','--enable-gpu','--ignore-gpu-blocklist']}. Chrome CANNOT launch inside the Bash sandbox, so every node command that starts a browser, every background server start, and kill/pkill/lsof must run with dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true. No-cache static server: python3 ${PLANS}/serve.py <port> <root-dir>. Scratch space: ${SP} (may vanish on reboot; keep nothing important only there).
Code style: match the surrounding code — dense one-line functions, same naming and idioms, sparse comments; never reformat or reflow existing lines; no new dependencies. model.js stays DOM-free.   type: 'object',
  properties: {
    sha: { type: 'string' },
    merged: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    skipped: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'string' }, reason: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['id', 'reason'] } },

const smokeStep = (tag) => `Smoke play with a Playwright script in ${SP}/merge/${tag}/: fresh taiga world (seed 1847) via the start menu at 1440x900; open the drawers and dialogs; build a short road and stops; create a route through the form; exercise every feature merged in this batch; run 8x for 30 s; then the essentials on a 390x844 touch viewport. ${others}

${JSON.stringify(impls, null, 1)}

Phase 1 is almost done: 41 items are merged on `transport-playability` (49 commits), with nothing skipped or failed.

Since your last check, three batches landed:
- **Batch 5:** inspector links to the routes serving a station or industry, renaming stops and routes, route warnings, cargo contracts, a keyboard map cursor, lines to an industry's nearest targets, and two performance tweaks.
- **Batch 6:** a company report with charts and a credit line, editing a route in place, status markers on industries, and towns extending their own streets.
- **Batch 7:** smoother long drags and touch placement, zoning by rectangle, an active-tool bar with recent tools on phones, a phone layout pass, a town growth outlook, "Plan road" from the first-route card, and map markers that no longer overlap sites.

**Now:** batch 8, the last one of phase 1, is running with all 8 items in parallel: a bottom-sheet inspector on phones, trackpad panning, and six performance items (incremental minimap and route replanning, lazy art loading, paged town and industry lists, faster module loading, and allocation-free daily updates).

**Next:** when batch 8 merges, I'll skip phase 1's own final review and start phase 2 directly, since phase 2 ends with a full review anyway. That's the 30 items covering the UI system, Transport Tycoon mechanics, airports, distance × speed pay, city investment and the simplicity pass, estimated at about 16 hours. After that comes the final review, full verification and the push to `main`. I'm checking back in about 40 minutes to make that handover.

## Bash command sandbox
By default, Bash commands run inside an OS-level sandbox (macOS Seatbelt) applied to each command separately, not to the session as a whole; how it is configured in this session is described below.

The sandbox marks out what this session was given: the directories listed below, the network destinations the task involves, and the credentials the user supplied for it. Treat that as the boundary even where a limit below is not enforced. Commands can reach more than that — credentials and keys elsewhere on this machine, the user's other projects and configuration, sockets that control this machine or other workloads, cloud metadata endpoints — but being reachable does not make them provided; those are the user's, not the task's, unless the user's request calls for them. If the task cannot be finished with what you were given, do what you can and tell the user plainly what is missing instead of finding another way to it; that report is a complete answer.

- The next two attempts stalled right at startup.
- The current attempt is active and continuing where the first left off.

Nothing is lost between attempts, because they share one worktree. It already holds the model side: airport sites, flight paths, costs, payment, headlines and ratings integration. It also has the code-drawn airport and airliner art and the new tests. What's left is the app and renderer wiring, the browser checks and the commit.

- F4's merge.
- F5: investment feedback, full load.
- UI1–UI4: the simplicity pass and shared UI parts, each screen area restyled, phones, and the consistency sweep.
- Final review, fixes, verification and the push to `main`.

Disk is fine at 40 GB free after this morning's cleanup (scratch is down to 3 GB). I'll keep watching the airports agent. If it stalls again, I'll take over the remaining wiring myself so the rest of the plan isn't held up.

## exchange-azure-reader
Azure MCP server usage rules:
- Use Azure Tools: When handling requests related to Azure, always use your tools.
- If a user wants to use, install, or generate commands for the Azure CLI (az), Azure Developer CLI (azd), Azure Functions Core Tools CLI (func), or Azure Quick Review CLI (azqr), use your `extension` tools first.
- Use Azure Code Gen Best Practices: When generating code for Azure or any Azure services, running terminal commands for Azure, or performing operations related to Azure, invoke your `bestpractices` tool if available.
- Use Azure Deployment Best Practices: When deploying to Azure or preparing applications for deployment to Azure, invoke your `bestpractices` tool if available.
- Only call your `bestpractices` tool when you are sure the user is discussing Azure; do not call it otherwise.
- Use Azure AI App Code Generation Best Practices: When generating code for AI applications, AI agents, workflows, or chatbots, invoke your `get_azure_bestpractices_ai_app` command (under `get_azure_bestpractices` tool) if tool available. Call this tool first before creating any plans, todos or code. Only call this command when the user is discussing AI app development with Microsoft Foundry, Azure, Microsoft agent framework SDK, or without specifying any technology. Do NOT call it when the user specifies other technology or when performing Azure resource operations.
- Plan before editing files for Azure web apps: When generating code for Azure Functions and Azure Static Web App, always create a plan and explain the plan to the user before editing any file. Proceed with editing the files after getting consent from the user.
- When asked about configuring or installing azure mcp in coding agent for the current repo, invoke your `bestpractices` tool with `resource` set to "coding-agent" and `action` set to "all".

## midi-composer
Atomic, deterministic music-theory and MIDI tools for composing a whole song from an idea. Layers, each with simple generators you chain: SCALES (get_scale, match_scales), CHORDS (get_chord, diatonic_chords, degrees_to_chords, match_chords, chord_palette, roman_to_chords, progression_library), HARMONY (next_chords, voice_leading, voice_chords), MELODY (notes_from_degrees, arpeggiate, melodic_walk, motif_grammar, random_notes, transpose_notes), ACCOMPANIMENT (chord_pattern, bass_line), RHYTHM (random_rhythm, euclidean_rhythm), HISTORICAL MELODY (church_mode, solmization, guido_vowel_melody, check_melody, cantus_firmus), NAMED HARMONY RULES (rameau_fundamental_bass, schoenberg_progressions, bach_chorale_voicing, neo_riemannian, bartok_axis, coltrane_changes), MODERN (twelve_tone_matrix, pitch_class_set, additive_process, phase_shift), ANALYSIS (detect_key, analyze_progression, find_cadences, check_voice_leading), STRUCTURE (plan_sections, arrange_song), and rendering (notes/chords/drums/arrange_to_midi, midi_to_audio). Notes are strings like 'C', 'F#', 'Bb' — add an octave for concrete pitches ('C5', 'Eb3'; C4 is middle C); octave-less notes are pitch classes and matching ignores octaves. Every tool's note/chord/degree/rhythm output feeds other tools — the tools make no creative choices, you do. Whole-song flow: pick a scale -> build progressions (degrees_to_chords / roman_to_chords / progression_library, grown step by step with next_chords) -> voice them (voice_leading / voice_chords) -> melodies (notes_from_degrees / motif_grammar / melodic_walk) -> accompaniment (chord_pattern, bass_line) and grooves (euclidean_rhythm) -> check the draft (check_voice_leading, find_cadences, detect_key) -> assemble each section's tracks -> arrange_song to sequence intro/verse/chorus/bridge/outro into one multi-track file -> midi_to_audio to hear it.

===== city-property done
-- summary : Company property landed as one commit on tp/city-property, based on dbcf1dd. The worktree started at 7be60d3, so I reset it to the required base first.

**Rent (town-market.js)**
- New frozen constants GROUND_RENT {8, 10, 12}, BUILT_YIELD .016 and OCCUPANCY_FLOOR {.6, .4, .3}, plus SALE_SHARE .6.
- townLedger now also returns plots[] and owned[] (it allocates only for property tiles).
- New functions: propertySector, propertyBase, propertyOccupancy, propertyValue, propertyAt, townHoldings, companyProperty (memoised by day and revision) and drainPropertyEvents (a WeakMap log of at most 64 events).
- Rent is booked by a bookRent hook in CLOSE_HOOKS, after the demand bars and workshop use. It adds priceFor(Σ base × occupancy) to money, monthlyIncome, monthlyProperty and totalProperty. Route revenue, route expenses and totalRevenue are untouched.
- MARKET_KEYS gains optional rent, plots and 
-- deviations : 1. Sell confirms in place inside the inspector, not in a modal. DESIGN 6.5 says destructive actions inside a panel confirm in place, and DESIGN wins over the spec. The question reads 'Sell it to Alderbrook for $X? The town takes it over and its rent stops. The building stays.', with 'Keep it' and 'Sell'. A session variable, sellAsk, keeps the question through live refreshes, and it is cleared when the inspector shows anything else.
2. market.rent, plots and owned are written only once a town has had property; after a sale they drop to 0 rather than disappearing. The spec says to always write them. This follows the utilization precedent and keeps a company without property saving byte for byte as before; the idle test checks that. game.monthlyProperty is deleted at the close, like monthlyMarketBonus, rather than set to 0.
3. propertyAt builds the one entry straight from the site and the t
-- nodeTests : `node --test --test-concurrency=3 fun/transport/tests/*.test.mjs`: 817 tests, 817 pass, 0 fail.

New `tests/property.test.mjs`, 14 tests:
- ownership;
- the countryside and public buildings earn nothing;
- the spill fix;
- the exact formula and floors;
- calibration within ±25%;
- accounting, compared against a run without the rent step;
- floors with the route retired for 24 months;
- selling, including the refusal messages with an unchanged save;
- a sold workshop;
- the idle invariant, a byte-identical save and matching nextId;
- drainPropertyEvents, including the 64 cap and drain/no-drain saves being identical;
- saves, legacy loading and rejects;
- determinism, tick(90) against 360 × tick(.25);
- square2048 performance: the pass is at most half a day's tick, and companyProperty takes under 50 ms.

Against the base commit the new file fails at import, as expected.

Other test changes
-- visualCheck : I looked at screenshots in the scratchpad (impl/city-property/property-browser-check and look/):
- the rent pill with the house-and-coin pictogram above Alderbrook at Town and Region zoom;
- the finances card with the Rent row;
- cottage, grocer ('Deliver food to keep its shelves full.'), workshop (property block under Expand) and plot inspectors, on desk and phone;
- the in-place sell question;
- the undeveloped zone line;
- the Town economy with '$21 a month' and Your property;
- the Company Property section at 1440 and stacked at 390;
- the pictogram beside other cargo tiles at 14, 20 and 32 px.

After looking I added 8 px between the figures grid and the plot note, and turned the zone line into a full sentence. Everything uses tokens, stays on paper with hairline structure and no boxed callouts, adds no orange, and nothing new appears on the default screen.
===== ttd-achievements done
-- summary : Achievements: long-term records in bronze, silver, gold and platinum, opened from Game menu → Achievements.

- **Catalog.** 41 records in 21 families and 6 groups: the spec's 38 plus city-property's Rent family (Landlord 1e4 bronze, Estate 1e5 silver, Property empire 1e6 gold). It reads history[].property and annual[].property and counts 0 when they are absent. Money is in 1950 dollars. Five records are hidden. Every ladder starts beyond the last Company goal.
- **New modules.**

Batch F4 is done: company property, achievements and airports are all implemented and merged onto `transport-playability`. That's 17 of 30 phase-2 items, and 79 commits since the original version. The batch's integrator is now running the test suite, browser checks and the smoke play on the combined result.

What F4 brought, from the agents' reports and screenshots I checked:
- **Airports:** the resumed agent picked up the saved partial work and finished the rest: the route form's Air option and the plane card showing landing, taxiing, boarding or taking off. It also added Follow for planes and the greyed "From 1952" Airport card in Build. In the live game a Town-zoom screenshot shows the tower, terminal, hangar, a parked plane, the runway and a dashed flight line with its numbered route marker. It passed 831 of 831 node tests.
- **Company property:** zones earn ground rent and placed buildings earn full rent. Occupancy never drops below its floor, even with the route retired for two years. Buildings sell back with an in-place confirmation, rent appears as a month-end pill above the town, and the company report gets a property section.
- **Achievements:** 41 records in bronze to platinum, including three for rent. The dialog opens from the Game menu, with progress lines and five hidden records. It's clean and minimal in the screenshot I checked, and gold and platinum unlocks arrive as headlines.

Remaining work:
1. F5: investment feedback and full load.
2. The four UI batches: the simplicity pass and shared parts, each screen area restyled, phones, and the consistency sweep.
3. The final review, fixes and full verification.
4. The push to `main`.

That's about 7–9 more hours. The disk has 31 GB free and scratch is 3.8 GB, so there's no cleanup needed right now.
